{"answer": "# Agent-Written Robot Code, Safeguards, AI-Designed Hardware, Provenance, and Evaluation for Laboratory Automation: A Literature Synthesis (2023–2026)

## 1. Agent-Written Robot Code on Physical Laboratory Hardware

The period 2023–2026 has seen a rapid expansion of systems executing language-model-generated code or plans on real laboratory robots, though quantitative reporting of success rates, failure modes, latency, cost, and human intervention remains inconsistent across the literature. The following table summarizes the key systems identified.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Coscientist** (Boiko et al., 2023) demonstrated autonomous design and execution of Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions on an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler. The system "autonomously designed, plans and performs complex experiments" and successfully verified target products by GC–MS analysis (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). It initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method but self-corrected after consulting documentation (pqac-00000040). Safety checking blocked hazardous suggestions including sodium azide as an additive and 220°C in ethanol (pqac-00000044). No aggregate success rate or trial count was reported; plates were moved manually (pqac-00000040).

**CLAIRify** (Yoshikawa et al., 2023) translated natural-language chemistry instructions into structured plans executed via constrained task-and-motion planning on a Franka robot. Constrained TAMP achieved 97% success with an 8-DoF robot versus 84% for 7-DoF; pouring relative errors were 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt (pqac-00000003). Failure modes included motion-planning failures, spillage, incorrect plan syntax, and perception errors (pqac-00000003).

**MATTERIX** (Darvish et al., 2025) provided a GPU-accelerated digital-twin framework for chemistry laboratories. Physical pick-and-place achieved 75% success (9/12 trials) with failures from pose estimation and calibration errors; liquid pouring achieved 90% (9/10) (pqac-00000032). The system validates workflows in a full simulated laboratory before physical execution (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036).

**LabscriptAI** (Gao et al., 2026; *bioRxiv preprint*) achieved a 96.7% simulation-pass rate on a 90-task liquid-handling benchmark—"the highest among the evaluated LLM-based and commercial baselines" (pqac-00000068). It supported four liquid-handling platforms (Opentrons OT-2, OT-Flex, Hamilton, Tecan Fluent) and demonstrated cross-platform reproducibility with CV below 5% and R² above 0.999 (pqac-00000052).

**WetRobo** (Oikawa et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) provided a reproducible robot kit for coding agents using PiPER arms. Cap removal was successfully adapted across two laboratories despite different grippers and camera placements; the initial adaptation took 2 h 40 min but repeat execution took only 3 min 27 s, illustrating the efficiency of code reuse (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024). An alternative VLA approach failed to transfer between sites (pqac-00000024).

**ACE-CaP-0** (2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 92.1% overall success (221/240 trials) across eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs, with no human or coding agent during evaluation. Mean physical execution time ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes per task (pqac-00000016).

**AMP1** (Bagherieh et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120 and 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO in simulation. Selected real-world tasks achieved 9/9 success with total times of 94–208 seconds (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020). Failure modes included grasp failures from object geometry/mass and "flaky verifiers rejecting valid end states" (pqac-00000020).

**SPINE** (Ham et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios (versus 99% for human operators using Claude Code) and reduced mean time-to-teleoperation by 38% (12 min 30 s to 7 min 48 s) (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). The strongest result was an 80% reduction in recovery time for disconnected camera and CAN links (pqac-00000049).

**Common failure modes** across systems include: hallucinated or deprecated API calls (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000040); perception and pose-estimation errors (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000032); grasp failures from object geometry (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020); wrong coordinate frames or units (pqac-00000032); prompt brittleness causing substantial performance variation (pqac-00000001); LLM "sleepwalking"—deviating from instructions without notification (pqac-00000001); and silent failures where VLM verifiers accepted failed states (pqac-00000004).

**Notable gap.** Per-task latency and monetary cost are almost universally unreported, as are human-intervention rates. Only ACE-CaP-0 and AMP1 report execution times systematically.

Subgoals should be "implementation-independent, count repeated achievements only once, and specify whether an achieved state must remain satisfied" (pqac-00000056). For the fixture-design component, relevant metrics include code-execution success, geometric accuracy (IoU, Chamfer distance), first-pass physical fit rate, iterations to successful function, and human edits required (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

### Baselines

Comparisons should include at minimum three conditions: (1) a human expert designing the fixture and writing the workflow from scratch; (2) a scripted or deterministic workflow baseline using pre-existing fixtures; and (3) the agent system (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000063). CaP-X explicitly compared CaP-Agent0 against human-written programs and found the agent matched or exceeded humans on 4 of 7 tasks (pqac-00000019). VABAR uses "human-specified workflow or graph baselines" alongside agent results (pqac-00000058).

### Sample Sizes

Current practice varies widely: ACE-CaP-0 used 30 trials per task (240 total) (pqac-00000016); CaP-Bench used 25 hardware trials per task (pqac-00000056); VoxPoser used 5 real tasks with 10 trials each; BUMBLE used 70 trials across three buildings (pqac-00000057). The literature recommends that "sample sizes should be large enough to support uncertainty estimates rather than relying on single runs" and should use Wilson intervals or Bayesian methods (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000061). For the proposed evaluation, **≥25 trials per task per condition** would align with current best practice, with reporting of confidence intervals.

### Expected Failure Rates

The literature suggests the following baseline expectations:
- **Best manipulation systems (frozen code):** 83–100% per-task success, 92% aggregate (ACE-CaP-0) (pqac-00000016)
- **Code-as-policy with perturbations:** 12–26% under position/instruction perturbations (CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO) (pqac-00000018)
- **Chemistry laboratory manipulation:** 75–90% for pick-and-place and pouring (MATTERIX) (pqac-00000032)
- **Sim-to-real gap:** simulation screening catches many failures but typically 10–15% of simulated successes fail on real hardware (pqac-00000004)
- **Safety violations:** policies exceeding 90% task success were unsafe in 18–28% of episodes; 38–56% of successful rollouts in one benchmark violated a safety clause (pqac-00000005)

### Evaluation Architecture

A defensible benchmark should: (1) use sealed or independently verifiable judges, separating diagnostic feedback from final evaluation (pqac-00000056); (2) deliberately inject execution-layer and sample-identity faults, scoring detection, localization, safe abort, recovery, and provenance preservation (pqac-00000059); (3) audit evaluator errors against references and report false acceptances and rejections separately (pqac-00000060); (4) freeze or explicitly measure any learning during testing (pqac-00000061); (5) test both simulation and physical embodiments with paired trials (pqac-00000058); and (6) disclose all human involvement including setup, resets, and reward code (pqac-00000057).

### For the Specific BYU Proposal

An evaluation of "agent designs fixture + writes workflow + arm runs it" is unprecedented in the literature. The closest analogs combine CADSmith-style computational CAD validation with ACE-CaP-0-style physical execution testing. A defensible protocol would:

1. **Fixture design:** Agent generates CadQuery code for each connecting part → geometric validation (IoU, Chamfer) → 3D print → measure dimensional accuracy → test fit on robot → score first-pass success, iterations, and human edits.
2. **Workflow writing:** Agent generates motion/manipulation code → simulation dry run → physical execution with ≥25 trials → score task success, safety violations, and latency.
3. **End-to-end:** Score the fraction of parts that fit, workflows that execute, and complete alloy-development loops that run without human handling, compared against human-designed fixtures and human-written workflows under matched conditions.
4. **Provenance:** Log every agent session, generated artifact, commit, and physical outcome in a hash-chained audit trail, then verify that the full chain can be reconstructed.

The literature suggests one should expect 75–92% physical success rates for well-developed manipulation tasks, significant iteration (2–5 cycles) for first-pass fixture fit, and that human intervention will be necessary for physical setup, safety checks, and debugging hardware faults that agents cannot diagnose remotely (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000032).

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

- **Per-task monetary cost** is essentially unreported across all systems.
- **Human-intervention frequency** is rarely quantified.
- **False-alarm rates** for individual safeguard layers are almost never measured.
- **AI-designed physical lab hardware** fabricated and tested on real robots: **no published evidence exists.**
- **ISO 10218:2025 cybersecurity clauses** have not been analyzed in the agent-lab literature.
- **Controlled comparison of frozen versus regenerated code** has not been published.
- **End-to-end agent-designed-fixture-plus-workflow evaluation** has no published precedent."}

Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab). Most remote work is done by AI coding agents: a GitHub comment starts an agent session in CI, which reaches a lab Raspberry Pi over SSH and drives the instrument (a gantry liquid handler, 3D printers, an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with Raspberry Pi cameras and AprilTags); risky actions such as starting a print wait for a human approval, and every session, command and result is recorded in the repository. The lab ran about 575 agent sessions in 30 days across seven repositories. A recent proposal of ours asks whether a language-model agent can design and validate the connecting hardware of an automated alloy-development loop (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers and fixtures, 3D-printed) and write the robot workflows around it, well enough that the loop runs with minimal human handling and full provenance. We have reproduced an agentic manipulation policy (Apple's AMP1, on the CaP-Gym benchmark) on a simulated PiPER; in simulation the agent measured and compensated joint deadbands on its own, but each task took minutes. We know of CaP-X/CaP-Gym, AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, WetRobo (a coding agent driving PiPER arms across two wet labs), Coscientist, CRESt, MATTERIX, LabSafety Bench and CADSmith.

Question.
(1) Agent-written robot code on physical laboratory hardware: which systems (2023 to 2026) have run language-model-generated code or plans on real lab robots or arms, with what measured success rates and trial counts, failure modes (unsafe or infeasible motions, wrong frames or units, hallucinated APIs, silent failures), latency and cost per task, and how often a human had to intervene?
(2) Safeguards: which verification layers have been shown to catch agent errors before or during execution (typed skill libraries, static checks, simulation or digital-twin dry runs, workspace and force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates), with measured catch rates and false-alarm rates? Is there evidence that freezing agent-written code once it works is more reliable than regenerating code for every run?
(3) Agent- or AI-designed physical hardware for laboratory robots: language-model or generative design of fixtures, holders, grippers, adapters or docking features that were then fabricated (for example 3D-printed) and tested on real hardware. Report first-pass fit or function rates, iterations to success, human edits needed, and how the designs were checked.
(4) Provenance and auditability for agent-operated laboratories: methods that link the request, the generated code or CAD, the commit, and the physical outcome (what was requested versus what physically happened), reproducibility of agent-run procedures across sites, and relevant standards (for example cybersecurity clauses in ISO 10218:2025 for networked robots).
(5) What would a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" look like: outcome metrics, baselines (human expert, scripted), sample sizes, and the failure rates the literature suggests we should expect?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, but include 2025 and 2026 preprints where they are the only evidence, flagged as preprints. For each claim give the DOI or arXiv ID and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Agent-Written Robot Code, Safeguards, AI-Designed Hardware, Provenance, and Evaluation for Laboratory Automation: A Literature Synthesis (2023–2026)

## 1. Agent-Written Robot Code on Physical Laboratory Hardware

The period 2023–2026 has seen a rapid expansion of systems executing language-model-generated code or plans on real laboratory robots, though quantitative reporting of success rates, failure modes, latency, cost, and human intervention remains inconsistent across the literature. The following table summarizes the key systems identified.

| System | Year / status | Hardware | Task domain | Measured success rate | Trial count | Key failure modes | Latency / cost | Human intervention | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Coscientist | 2023, peer reviewed | Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler and heater–shaker; GC–MS used for outcome verification | Chemical synthesis and reaction planning | Qualitative physical success: target products verified for both Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira couplings; no defensible aggregate success rate reported | Not reported | Initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method; corrected after documentation retrieval; plates were moved manually | Not reported | No human decision-making reported, but humans manually transferred plates | DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06792-0 (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 6-6) |
| CLAIRify | 2023, peer reviewed | Franka arm with laboratory tools | Chemistry plans, pouring, solubility and recrystallization | Constrained TAMP: 97% with an 8-DoF configuration and 84% with 7 DoF; pouring relative error 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt; solubility-estimation error 7.2% | Trial denominator not reported in retrieved evidence | Invalid plan syntax or constraints, motion-planning failure, perception error, spillage and manipulation/state-assessment errors | Not reported | Intervention frequency not reported | DOI: 10.1007/s10514-023-10136-2 (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4) |
| AILA / AFMBench | 2024 preprint; 2025 peer reviewed | Atomic-force microscope | Autonomous microscopy: calibration, imaging and property measurement | Reported above 80% on multi-step workflows; exact physical trial denominator and task-level rates not available in retrieved evidence | Not reported | Prompt brittleness, wrong agent/tool selection, misunderstood context, deviation from instructions (“sleepwalking”) and actions outside requirements | Not reported | Not reported | DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-64105-7; arXiv:2501.10385 (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15) |
| MATTERIX | 2025, peer reviewed | Franka FR3 plus Opentrons OT-2 and digital twin | Chemistry-lab manipulation and liquid handling | Physical pick-and-place: 75% (9/12); physical pouring: 90% (9/10) | 22 reported physical trials across those two tests | Pose-estimation and calibration errors, wrong object frames, action failures, mismatched digital/physical assets, vessel/workspace discrepancies | Not reported | Not reported; policies were developed in simulation and transferred to hardware | DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14) |
| LabscriptAI | 2026, **bioRxiv preprint** | Opentrons OT-2/Flex, Hamilton platforms, Tecan Fluent and associated modules | Synthetic-biology liquid handling and protocol translation | 96.7% simulator-pass rate on a 90-task benchmark; physical cross-platform calibration produced CV below 5% and R² above 0.999, but no aggregate physical success rate | 90 simulated benchmark tasks; large physical campaigns included 318 GFP variants and 399 enzyme variants | Simulator/API validation errors; inadequate protein purification in one workflow; broader instrument integration remained incomplete | Per-task latency and monetary cost not reported | Human-in-the-loop dialogue validates protocols; intervention frequency not reported | DOI: 10.1101/2025.09.30.679666 (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 1-4, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 15-18, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7) |
| WetRobo | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | AgileX PiPER arms with cameras and laboratory end effectors | Wet-lab manipulation: dish lids, caps and incubator doors | Qualitative success on real robots; cap-removal code adapted successfully in two laboratories with different grippers and camera placement; no aggregate rate | Individual adaptation trials; denominator not reported | Slipping after lid lifting, limited equipment/site generality and untested dish transport | Door opening: 2 h 40 min initial agent adaptation versus 3 min 27 s repeat execution; token/energy cost noted but not quantified | Reduced need for local teleoperation; exact intervention rate not reported | arXiv:2609.18435 (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9, oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2) |
| CaP-Agent0 / CaP-X | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Robot-manipulation stack including Franka-compatible real-robot interface; principal quoted metric is simulated LIBERO-PRO | General manipulation via agent-written policies | LIBERO-PRO averages: 11.8–25.6% under position perturbations and 14.0–18.2% under instruction perturbations; these are not physical-lab success rates | 50 trials per task in LIBERO-PRO | Mis-segmentation, occlusion, angled or failed grasps, control-API failures and collisions from absent collision-aware planning | Not reported | Not reported | arXiv:2603.22435 (fu2026capxaframework pages 56-58, fu2026capxaframework pages 7-8) |
| SPINE | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Four AgileX PiPER 6-DoF arms, ROS/CAN and RealSense cameras | Cyber-physical diagnosis and restoration of robot teleoperation | 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios versus 99% for human operators | 5 fault scenarios | Software/configuration faults, disconnected cameras or CAN links, cable/controller faults and hybrid hardware–software failures | Mean recovery 7 min 48 s versus 12 min 30 s for humans: 38% faster; cost not reported | Novice operator remained necessary for physical actions and observations | arXiv:2607.13049 (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 3-5) |
| AMP1 | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Real robot arm plus CaP-Gym simulated embodiments | General manipulation using agent-written, self-revising policies | Simulation: 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120, 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO, 100% on robosuite and 96.0% on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks; selected real tasks achieved 9/9 each | Selected physical tasks: 9 trials each; complete total not reported in retrieved evidence | Grasp failures from geometry/mass, flaky verifiers rejecting valid states and controller interruptions; AMP1 included error recovery | Selected physical tasks averaged 94–208 s; 34.8 model calls per simulated episode with full sensing; monetary cost not reported | Human-intervention rate not reported | arXiv:2611.09892 (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 4-5, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4) |
| ACE-CaP-0 | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Real robot-arm manipulation platform | Eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs | 92.1% overall (221/240); task rates 83.3–100% | 30 trials per task; 240 total | Paper excerpt reports unsuccessful trials but no qualitative failure taxonomy | Mean physical execution 0.97–2.27 min per task; monetary cost not reported | No human or coding agent during evaluation; development allowed at most 10 human-assisted scene resets per task | arXiv:2611.16872 (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12) |


*Table: Systems that executed language-model-generated plans or code on laboratory or manipulation hardware, with simulation-only metrics clearly distinguished from physical trials. Missing latency, cost, and intervention values are marked rather than inferred.*

**Coscientist** (Boiko et al., 2023) demonstrated autonomous design and execution of Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions on an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler. The system "autonomously designed, plans and performs complex experiments" and successfully verified target products by GC–MS analysis (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 1-2). It initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method but self-corrected after consulting documentation (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6). Safety checking blocked hazardous suggestions including sodium azide as an additive and 220°C in ethanol (ezeh2026acomprehensivereview pages 33-37). No aggregate success rate or trial count was reported; plates were moved manually (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6).

**CLAIRify** (Yoshikawa et al., 2023) translated natural-language chemistry instructions into structured plans executed via constrained task-and-motion planning on a Franka robot. Constrained TAMP achieved 97% success with an 8-DoF robot versus 84% for 7-DoF; pouring relative errors were 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4). Failure modes included motion-planning failures, spillage, incorrect plan syntax, and perception errors (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4).

**MATTERIX** (Darvish et al., 2025) provided a GPU-accelerated digital-twin framework for chemistry laboratories. Physical pick-and-place achieved 75% success (9/12 trials) with failures from pose estimation and calibration errors; liquid pouring achieved 90% (9/10) (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14). The system validates workflows in a full simulated laboratory before physical execution (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 9-11).

**LabscriptAI** (Gao et al., 2026; *bioRxiv preprint*) achieved a 96.7% simulation-pass rate on a 90-task liquid-handling benchmark—"the highest among the evaluated LLM-based and commercial baselines" (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7). It supported four liquid-handling platforms (Opentrons OT-2, OT-Flex, Hamilton, Tecan Fluent) and demonstrated cross-platform reproducibility with CV below 5% and R² above 0.999 (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15).

**WetRobo** (Oikawa et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) provided a reproducible robot kit for coding agents using PiPER arms. Cap removal was successfully adapted across two laboratories despite different grippers and camera placements; the initial adaptation took 2 h 40 min but repeat execution took only 3 min 27 s, illustrating the efficiency of code reuse (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9, oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2). An alternative VLA approach failed to transfer between sites (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2).

**ACE-CaP-0** (2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 92.1% overall success (221/240 trials) across eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs, with no human or coding agent during evaluation. Mean physical execution time ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes per task (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12).

**AMP1** (Bagherieh et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120 and 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO in simulation. Selected real-world tasks achieved 9/9 success with total times of 94–208 seconds (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 4-5, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4). Failure modes included grasp failures from object geometry/mass and "flaky verifiers rejecting valid end states" (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4).

**SPINE** (Ham et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios (versus 99% for human operators using Claude Code) and reduced mean time-to-teleoperation by 38% (12 min 30 s to 7 min 48 s) (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7). The strongest result was an 80% reduction in recovery time for disconnected camera and CAN links (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7).

**Common failure modes** across systems include: hallucinated or deprecated API calls (inagaki2023llmscangenerate pages 1-3, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6); perception and pose-estimation errors (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14); grasp failures from object geometry (fu2026capxaframework pages 56-58, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4); wrong coordinate frames or units (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14); prompt brittleness causing substantial performance variation (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15); LLM "sleepwalking"—deviating from instructions without notification (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15); and silent failures where VLM verifiers accepted failed states (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37).

**Notable gap.** Per-task latency and monetary cost are almost universally unreported, as are human-intervention rates. Only ACE-CaP-0 and AMP1 report execution times systematically.

## 2. Safeguards and Verification Layers

The following table summarizes the verification layers demonstrated in the literature.

| Safeguard layer | System / method | Mechanism | Measured effectiveness | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Static / formal checks | NeSyRo | Validates generated code with an SMT solver, checks skill preconditions with a PDDL planner, and generates probes for missing observations. | Real-robot average success was **57.5% versus 10.6%** for Code as Policies; **7 versus 53 irreversible actions**. | (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18) |
| Static / formal checks | Lang2LTL | Translates natural-language commands into temporal logic and aborts plans whose constraints are unsatisfiable. | Evaluated **52 commands**, including **12 unsatisfiable commands**, all of which were aborted. False-rejection rate was not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Static / formal checks | VASO | Model-checks induced plans against temporal-logic safety specifications using an automatically generated state-to-proposition mapping. | **96.8% specification compliance** with automatic mapping and **97.2%** with handcrafted mapping; guarantees depend on mapping correctness. | (li2026whentheworld pages 44-46) |
| Simulation / digital-twin dry run | MATTERIX | Executes hierarchical workflows in a GPU-based chemistry-laboratory digital twin, checking motion, semantic preconditions, liquids, heat transfer, and approximate reaction state before sim-to-real deployment. | Subsequent physical tests achieved **9/12 pick-and-place** and **9/10 pouring** successes; no controlled catch-rate or false-alarm comparison was reported. | (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 9-11) |
| Simulation / digital-twin dry run | ReSkill | Develops and screens programs in simulation before deploying the selected program without regeneration on hardware. | **72/80 simulated successes versus 62/80 real successes**, showing both screening value and a residual sim-to-real gap. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Simulation / API validation | LabscriptAI | Runs generated scripts in platform-specific simulators; a reviewer returns errors to a coder that applies targeted patches rather than regenerating the entire script. | Maximum of nine repair iterations; the paper reports **96.7% simulation-pass rate on 90 tasks**, but no physical-error catch rate or false-alarm rate. | (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7) |
| Runtime monitor | Code-as-Monitor | Generates a VLM-based checker for spatiotemporal constraints and replans only after detecting a violation. | **88.33% success versus 76.67%** for a continuously queried baseline in simulated block stacking; explicit monitor sensitivity and false-alarm rates were not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18) |
| Runtime safety filter | RoboGuard | Applies an external safety layer that rejects unsafe actions even when the underlying model is jailbroken. | Reduced unsafe execution under worst-case jailbreaks from **over 92% to below 3%**. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Runtime multi-stage gates | LEASH | Separates task-level, action-level, and gripper/pouring safety gates before releasing actions. | On 92 RoboRisk tasks, reduced harm for one model from **11.23% to 0.00%** and for another from **61.23% to 12.68%**; false-alarm rate was not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 39-40) |
| VLM safety monitor | Chemist Eye | Uses vision-language models to detect PPE violations, accidents, and possible fires and to recommend robot or human responses. | Aggregate **97% hazard spotting** and **95% decision performance**; PPE accuracy ranged from **67.5% to 97.5%**, with format-hallucination rates of **0–1%**. Conventional false-positive rates were not reported. | (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 7-8, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 5-6, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 1-2) |
| Safety benchmark—not an execution safeguard | LabSafety Bench | Tests whether LLMs and VLMs identify hazards and consequences in structured questions and realistic laboratory scenarios. | Across 19 models, **none exceeded 70% accuracy** on realistic hazard identification, arguing against using an unaided LLM as a safety gate. | (zhou2026benchmarkinglargelanguage pages 9-12, zhou2026benchmarkinglargelanguage pages 2-4, zhou2026benchmarkinglargelanguage pages 1-2) |
| Human approval and audit gate | La Agente Óptima | Authenticates individual users, distinguishes technician and autonomous-system identities, and records state transitions in an append-only SHA-256 hash-chained ledger; operator approval can authorize hardware release. | Tamper-evident attribution and reconstruction are demonstrated architecturally; no measured error-catch, approval, or false-alarm rate was reported. | (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 54-55, li2026whentheworld pages 37-39) |
| Human-guided physical intervention | SPINE | Separates software repair from operator-executed physical actions, then requires fresh end-to-end teleoperation and hidden-readiness checks before closure. | Resolved **all five PiPER fault scenarios** and reduced mean recovery time by **38%**; a human remained necessary for cables, devices, observations, and other physical actions. | (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 3-5) |
| Human-in-the-loop protocol gate | LabscriptAI | Requires dialogue to validate and refine the natural-language protocol before code generation, followed by simulator review and iterative patching. | Physical cross-platform calibration achieved **CV below 5%** and **R² above 0.999**; the frequency and error-catch rate of human interventions were not reported. | (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7) |
| Workspace / geofence limit | DroneServer | Declines or blocks commands that would violate a configured geographic safety envelope. | The model declined **48 of 110** violating commands and the server blocked the remaining **62**, producing **zero zone escapes**. This measures geofencing, not force limiting. | (li2026whentheworld pages 39-40) |
| Frozen-code reuse | WetRobo | Preserves the adapted robot program and reuses it for later runs instead of repeating agent exploration and code generation. | Incubator-door opening took **2 h 40 min** during initial adaptation but **3 min 27 s** on repeat execution; reliability trial counts were not reported. | (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9) |
| Frozen-code evaluation | ACE-CaP-0 | Freezes agent-developed programs before evaluation; neither a coding agent nor a human modifies them during test trials. | **92.1% success (221/240)** over eight real-world tasks, with no human intervention during evaluation. This supports reliable reuse but is not a randomized comparison against per-run regeneration. | (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12) |


*Table: Safeguards for agent-generated robot code, including formal checks, simulation, runtime monitoring, human gates, safety envelopes, and frozen-code reuse. Quantitative results are shown where published; missing catch and false-alarm rates are identified explicitly.*

### Key Findings

**Static and formal checks** represent the most rigorous pre-execution layer. NeSyRo improved real-robot success from 10.6% (Code as Policies) to 57.5% and reduced irreversible actions from 53 to 7 by validating generated code with an SMT solver and checking skill preconditions with a PDDL planner (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18). VASO achieved 96.8% specification compliance by model-checking plans against temporal-logic safety specifications (li2026whentheworld pages 44-46).

**Simulation dry runs** are the most widely used safeguard. MATTERIX validates entire chemistry workflows—including robotic manipulation, chemical kinetics, and heat transfer—in a digital twin before physical execution (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5). LabscriptAI uses platform-specific simulators with iterative targeted patching rather than full regeneration (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7). ReSkill demonstrated that simulation screening catches many errors but leaves a residual gap: 72/80 simulated successes versus 62/80 real successes (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37).

**Runtime safety filters** can dramatically reduce unsafe behavior. RoboGuard reduced unsafe execution under worst-case jailbreaks from over 92% to below 3% (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37). LEASH used separate task, action, and gripper/pouring gates to reduce harm from 11.23% to 0.00% for one model on 92 RoboRisk tasks (li2026whentheworld pages 39-40). However, VLM-based runtime verifiers can be unreliable: one fixed VLM "accepted 50.0% of remaining hover failures" and a learned verifier "was wrong on 91% of 699 later rollouts" (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37).

**Vision-language safety monitors** show promise but are not yet reliable for autonomous decisions. Chemist Eye achieved 97% aggregate hazard spotting and 95% decision-making performance in a self-driving chemistry laboratory (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 1-2), with PPE detection accuracy ranging from 67.5% to 97.5% depending on query format (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 5-6). LabSafety Bench found that no evaluated model—across 19 LLMs and VLMs—exceeded 70% accuracy on realistic hazard identification, "highlighting significant safety challenges" (zhou2026benchmarkinglargelanguage pages 9-12, zhou2026benchmarkinglargelanguage pages 1-2).

**Human approval gates** remain essential. La Agente Óptima implements authenticated API keys, operator certification, and an append-only SHA-256 hash-chained audit ledger (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 54-55). SPINE requires human operators for physical actions and validates recovery through end-to-end teleoperation checks (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3). The emerging consensus is that "human judgment remains necessary" for safety-critical decisions (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 7-8).

**Frozen versus regenerated code.** No controlled randomized comparison exists, but indirect evidence favors freezing. ACE-CaP-0 achieved 92.1% with frozen programs and no agent during evaluation (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12). WetRobo showed that reusing generated code reduced execution from 2 h 40 min to 3 min 27 s (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9). RHO deploys single-turn frozen programs at test time (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18). However, online revision can be "much more successful than one-shot execution in some settings, so freezing is not universally more reliable" (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18). The practical recommendation is to freeze code once validated and implement regression testing when the library changes (li2026whentheworld pages 44-46, li2026whentheworld pages 57-59).

**Missing evidence.** Catch rates and false-alarm rates for most individual safeguard layers are unreported. No study systematically measures the precision and recall of human approval gates (cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 8-11, li2026whentheworld pages 57-59).

## 3. Agent- or AI-Designed Physical Hardware for Laboratory Robots

**This is the area with the largest evidence gap.** No published study was found in which a language model or generative-AI system designed a laboratory fixture, holder, gripper, adapter, or docking feature that was then 3D-printed and tested on real laboratory robot hardware, with reported first-pass fit rates, iterations to success, or human edits needed.

The closest evidence comes from **text-to-CAD generation** systems evaluated computationally:

- **CADSmith** (Barkley et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) used five agents and two nested correction loops (inner for code errors, outer for geometric validation using OpenCASCADE measurements and VLM judgment). It achieved 100% execution rate on a 100-prompt benchmark and improved median IoU from 0.8085 to 0.9629 and reduced mean Chamfer Distance from 28.37 to 0.74 (barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 1-2, barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 6-7). Failure modes included "structurally incorrect yet geometrically valid solids" and subtle gaps missed by fixed viewing angles (barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 7-8). No physical fabrication or testing was reported (barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 1-2).

- **IterCAD** (Hu et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 0.64% invalid ratio (~99.36% code validity) and low median Chamfer distance of 0.10 on Text2CAD benchmarks (hu2026itercadaniterative pages 8-10). Its iterative multimodal correction averaged 2.34 turns per design. No physical validation was reported.

- **AgentsCAD** (George et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) specifically targeted design-for-manufacturing of FDM parts using multi-agent LLM reasoning, but was evaluated computationally.

**3D-printed laboratory components** are widely documented in the self-driving-lab literature. Doloi et al. (2025) reviewed advances in low-cost 3D printing for laboratory automation, including "automatic liquid handlers, robotic arms, automated" components. However, these designs were human-engineered rather than AI-generated.

**Implication for the BYU proposal.** The proposal to have an agent design connecting hardware (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers) would represent genuinely novel work. The closest precedent is CADSmith's computational CAD generation pipeline, which could be extended to lab-fixture design with physical validation. The expected workflow would involve: LLM generates CadQuery/OpenSCAD code → geometric validation loop → 3D printing → physical fit testing → iteration. Based on CADSmith's computational results, one might expect high code-execution rates but significant iteration for dimensional accuracy and functional fit, requiring human measurement feedback.

## 4. Provenance and Auditability for Agent-Operated Laboratories

### Demonstrated Approaches

**Git-based provenance.** WetRobo packages the robot's base stack, skill instructions (AGENTS.md), and agent-generated programs in a Git repository, with trial snapshots retained as branches. This creates a "record linking the starting software, agent-generated modifications, and individual attempts" (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2). However, it does not include signed commits, immutable logs, or formal linkage from commits to measured physical outcomes (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2).

**Hash-chained audit ledger.** La Agente Óptima implements the most rigorous provenance: "all robot state transitions pass through one funnel that atomically persists state and appends a line-delimited JSON entry to an append-only, hash-chained audit ledger. Each entry records the actor, action, structured payload, UTC timestamp, predecessor hash, and SHA-256 hashes of the complete state before and after the transition" (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 54-55). This enables reconstruction of "the requesting person, technician certification of the physical deck, autonomous actions between request and measurement, and whether the record was altered" (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 54-55).

**Community database deposition.** LabscriptAI deposits experimental data with metadata to FPBase (excitation/emission spectra, quantum yields) and EnzymeML (raw kinetics data), providing "traceability and reproducibility at the protocol/data level" (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 15-18).

**Digital-twin synchronization.** MATTERIX synchronizes the simulated and real robots via FoundationPose-based pose estimation, enabling comparison of predicted and actual outcomes (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 9-11). This provides a form of "what was planned versus what happened" comparison, though quantitative discrepancy metrics were not systematically reported.

### Cross-Site Reproducibility

WetRobo demonstrated cross-site reproducibility for cap removal across two laboratories with different grippers and camera placements; the coding-agent approach succeeded while a VLA baseline failed to transfer (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2). LabscriptAI demonstrated cross-platform protocol translation with calibration CV below 5% across four liquid-handling platforms (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15). These represent the strongest published demonstrations, though both involve limited task sets.

### Standards

**No retrieved publication specifically discusses ISO 10218:2025 or its cybersecurity clauses for networked robots in the context of agent-operated laboratories.** The 2025 revision of ISO 10218 (Parts 1 and 2) added requirements for cybersecurity of networked industrial robot systems, but the agent-lab literature has not yet engaged with these requirements. Cheng et al. (2026) call generally for "cybersecurity and AI-security practices" but name no specific standard (cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 11-13). The proposed design principles—authenticated identity, state provenance, human certification, and tamper-evident audit trails (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 54-55)—align with the spirit of ISO 10218:2025 but have not been evaluated against its specific clauses.

## 5. Defensible Evaluation Design

Based on the surveyed literature, a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" should include the following elements:

### Outcome Metrics

Evaluations should report binary task success, quantitative partial progress through task-defined subgoals, safety violations, execution cost (model calls, tokens, GPU time, robot time), wall-clock time, and uncertainty intervals over repeated trials (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52). Subgoals should be "implementation-independent, count repeated achievements only once, and specify whether an achieved state must remain satisfied" (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52). For the fixture-design component, relevant metrics include code-execution success, geometric accuracy (IoU, Chamfer distance), first-pass physical fit rate, iterations to successful function, and human edits required (barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 1-2, barkley2603cadsmithmultiagentcad pages 6-7).

### Baselines

Comparisons should include at minimum three conditions: (1) a human expert designing the fixture and writing the workflow from scratch; (2) a scripted or deterministic workflow baseline using pre-existing fixtures; and (3) the agent system (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52, li2026whentheworld pages 49-51, wang2025thedawnof pages 21-23). CaP-X explicitly compared CaP-Agent0 against human-written programs and found the agent matched or exceeded humans on 4 of 7 tasks (fu2026capxaframework pages 7-8). VABAR uses "human-specified workflow or graph baselines" alongside agent results (li2026whentheworld pages 49-51).

### Sample Sizes

Current practice varies widely: ACE-CaP-0 used 30 trials per task (240 total) (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12); CaP-Bench used 25 hardware trials per task (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52); VoxPoser used 5 real tasks with 10 trials each; BUMBLE used 70 trials across three buildings (wang2026asurveyof pages 11-12). The literature recommends that "sample sizes should be large enough to support uncertainty estimates rather than relying on single runs" and should use Wilson intervals or Bayesian methods (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52, li2026whentheworld pages 54-55). For the proposed evaluation, **≥25 trials per task per condition** would align with current best practice, with reporting of confidence intervals.

### Expected Failure Rates

The literature suggests the following baseline expectations:
- **Best manipulation systems (frozen code):** 83–100% per-task success, 92% aggregate (ACE-CaP-0) (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12)
- **Code-as-policy with perturbations:** 12–26% under position/instruction perturbations (CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO) (fu2026capxaframework pages 56-58)
- **Chemistry laboratory manipulation:** 75–90% for pick-and-place and pouring (MATTERIX) (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14)
- **Sim-to-real gap:** simulation screening catches many failures but typically 10–15% of simulated successes fail on real hardware (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37)
- **Safety violations:** policies exceeding 90% task success were unsafe in 18–28% of episodes; 38–56% of successful rollouts in one benchmark violated a safety clause (li2026whentheworld pages 37-39)

### Evaluation Architecture

A defensible benchmark should: (1) use sealed or independently verifiable judges, separating diagnostic feedback from final evaluation (li2026whentheworld pages 51-52); (2) deliberately inject execution-layer and sample-identity faults, scoring detection, localization, safe abort, recovery, and provenance preservation (cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 11-13); (3) audit evaluator errors against references and report false acceptances and rejections separately (li2026whentheworld pages 55-57); (4) freeze or explicitly measure any learning during testing (li2026whentheworld pages 54-55); (5) test both simulation and physical embodiments with paired trials (li2026whentheworld pages 49-51); and (6) disclose all human involvement including setup, resets, and reward code (wang2026asurveyof pages 11-12).

### For the Specific BYU Proposal

An evaluation of "agent designs fixture + writes workflow + arm runs it" is unprecedented in the literature. The closest analogs combine CADSmith-style computational CAD validation with ACE-CaP-0-style physical execution testing. A defensible protocol would:

1. **Fixture design:** Agent generates CadQuery code for each connecting part → geometric validation (IoU, Chamfer) → 3D print → measure dimensional accuracy → test fit on robot → score first-pass success, iterations, and human edits.
2. **Workflow writing:** Agent generates motion/manipulation code → simulation dry run → physical execution with ≥25 trials → score task success, safety violations, and latency.
3. **End-to-end:** Score the fraction of parts that fit, workflows that execute, and complete alloy-development loops that run without human handling, compared against human-designed fixtures and human-written workflows under matched conditions.
4. **Provenance:** Log every agent session, generated artifact, commit, and physical outcome in a hash-chained audit trail, then verify that the full chain can be reconstructed.

The literature suggests one should expect 75–92% physical success rates for well-developed manipulation tasks, significant iteration (2–5 cycles) for first-pass fixture fit, and that human intervention will be necessary for physical setup, safety checks, and debugging hardware faults that agents cannot diagnose remotely (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14).

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

- **Per-task monetary cost** is essentially unreported across all systems.
- **Human-intervention frequency** is rarely quantified.
- **False-alarm rates** for individual safeguard layers are almost never measured.
- **AI-designed physical lab hardware** fabricated and tested on real robots: **no published evidence exists.**
- **ISO 10218:2025 cybersecurity clauses** have not been analyzed in the agent-lab literature.
- **Controlled comparison of frozen versus regenerated code** has not been published.
- **End-to-end agent-designed-fixture-plus-workflow evaluation** has no published precedent.

## 1. Agent-Written Robot Code on Physical Laboratory Hardware

The period 2023–2026 has seen a rapid expansion of systems executing language-model-generated code or plans on real laboratory robots, though quantitative reporting of success rates, failure modes, latency, cost, and human intervention remains inconsistent across the literature. **Coscientist** (Boiko et al., 2023) demonstrated autonomous design and execution of Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions on an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler. The system "autonomously designed, plans and performs complex experiments" and successfully verified target products by GC–MS analysis (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). It initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method but self-corrected after consulting documentation (pqac-00000040). Safety checking blocked hazardous suggestions including sodium azide as an additive and 220°C in ethanol (pqac-00000044). No aggregate success rate or trial count was reported; plates were moved manually (pqac-00000040).

**CLAIRify** (Yoshikawa et al., 2023) translated natural-language chemistry instructions into structured plans executed via constrained task-and-motion planning on a Franka robot. Constrained TAMP achieved 97% success with an 8-DoF robot versus 84% for 7-DoF; pouring relative errors were 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt (pqac-00000003). Failure modes included motion-planning failures, spillage, incorrect plan syntax, and perception errors (pqac-00000003).

**MATTERIX** (Darvish et al., 2025) provided a GPU-accelerated digital-twin framework for chemistry laboratories. Physical pick-and-place achieved 75% success (9/12 trials) with failures from pose estimation and calibration errors; liquid pouring achieved 90% (9/10) (pqac-00000032). The system validates workflows in a full simulated laboratory before physical execution (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036).

**LabscriptAI** (Gao et al., 2026; *bioRxiv preprint*) achieved a 96.7% simulation-pass rate on a 90-task liquid-handling benchmark—"the highest among the evaluated LLM-based and commercial baselines" (pqac-00000068). It supported four liquid-handling platforms (Opentrons OT-2, OT-Flex, Hamilton, Tecan Fluent) and demonstrated cross-platform reproducibility with CV below 5% and R² above 0.999 (pqac-00000052).

**WetRobo** (Oikawa et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) provided a reproducible robot kit for coding agents using PiPER arms. Cap removal was successfully adapted across two laboratories despite different grippers and camera placements; the initial adaptation took 2 h 40 min but repeat execution took only 3 min 27 s, illustrating the efficiency of code reuse (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024). An alternative VLA approach failed to transfer between sites (pqac-00000024).

**ACE-CaP-0** (2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 92.1% overall success (221/240 trials) across eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs, with no human or coding agent during evaluation. Mean physical execution time ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes per task (pqac-00000016).

**AMP1** (Bagherieh et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120 and 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO in simulation. Selected real-world tasks achieved 9/9 success with total times of 94–208 seconds (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020). Failure modes included grasp failures from object geometry/mass and "flaky verifiers rejecting valid end states" (pqac-00000020).

**SPINE** (Ham et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios (versus 99% for human operators using Claude Code) and reduced mean time-to-teleoperation by 38% (12 min 30 s to 7 min 48 s) (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). The strongest result was an 80% reduction in recovery time for disconnected camera and CAN links (pqac-00000049).

**Common failure modes** across systems include: hallucinated or deprecated API calls (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000040); perception and pose-estimation errors (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000032); grasp failures from object geometry (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020); wrong coordinate frames or units (pqac-00000032); prompt brittleness causing substantial performance variation (pqac-00000001); LLM "sleepwalking"—deviating from instructions without notification (pqac-00000001); and silent failures where VLM verifiers accepted failed states (pqac-00000004).

**Notable gap.** Per-task latency and monetary cost are almost universally unreported, as are human-intervention rates. Only ACE-CaP-0 and AMP1 report execution times systematically.

| Workspace / geofence limit | DroneServer | Declines or blocks commands that would violate a configured geographic safety envelope. | The model declined **48 of 110** violating commands and the server blocked the remaining **62**, producing **zero zone escapes**. This measures geofencing, not force limiting. | (pqac-00000007) |
| Frozen-code reuse | WetRobo | Preserves the adapted robot program and reuses it for later runs instead of repeating agent exploration and code generation. | Incubator-door opening took **2 h 40 min** during initial adaptation but **3 min 27 s** on repeat execution; reliability trial counts were not reported. | (pqac-00000002) |
| Frozen-code evaluation | ACE-CaP-0 | Freezes agent-developed programs before evaluation; neither a coding agent nor a human modifies them during test trials. | **92.1% success (221/240)** over eight real-world tasks, with no human intervention during evaluation. This supports reliable reuse but is not a randomized comparison against per-run regeneration. | (pqac-00000016) |


*Table: Safeguards for agent-generated robot code, including formal checks, simulation, runtime monitoring, human gates, safety envelopes, and frozen-code reuse. Quantitative results are shown where published; missing catch and false-alarm rates are identified explicitly.*

### Key Findings

**Static and formal checks** represent the most rigorous pre-execution layer. NeSyRo improved real-robot success from 10.6% (Code as Policies) to 57.5% and reduced irreversible actions from 53 to 7 by validating generated code with an SMT solver and checking skill preconditions with a PDDL planner (pqac-00000006). VASO achieved 96.8% specification compliance by model-checking plans against temporal-logic safety specifications (pqac-00000009).

**Simulation dry runs** are the most widely used safeguard. MATTERIX validates entire chemistry workflows—including robotic manipulation, chemical kinetics, and heat transfer—in a digital twin before physical execution (pqac-00000034). LabscriptAI uses platform-specific simulators with iterative targeted patching rather than full regeneration (pqac-00000068). ReSkill demonstrated that simulation screening catches many errors but leaves a residual gap: 72/80 simulated successes versus 62/80 real successes (pqac-00000004).

**Runtime safety filters** can dramatically reduce unsafe behavior. RoboGuard reduced unsafe execution under worst-case jailbreaks from over 92% to below 3% (pqac-00000004). LEASH used separate task, action, and gripper/pouring gates to reduce harm from 11.23% to 0.00% for one model on 92 RoboRisk tasks (pqac-00000007). However, VLM-based runtime verifiers can be unreliable: one fixed VLM "accepted 50.0% of remaining hover failures" and a learned verifier "was wrong on 91% of 699 later rollouts" (pqac-00000004).

**Vision-language safety monitors** show promise but are not yet reliable for autonomous decisions. Chemist Eye achieved 97% aggregate hazard spotting and 95% decision-making performance in a self-driving chemistry laboratory (pqac-00000067), with PPE detection accuracy ranging from 67.5% to 97.5% depending on query format (pqac-00000066). LabSafety Bench found that no evaluated model—across 19 LLMs and VLMs—exceeded 70% accuracy on realistic hazard identification, "highlighting significant safety challenges" (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

**Human approval gates** remain essential. La Agente Óptima implements authenticated API keys, operator certification, and an append-only SHA-256 hash-chained audit ledger (pqac-00000026). SPINE requires human operators for physical actions and validates recovery through end-to-end teleoperation checks (pqac-00000046). The emerging consensus is that "human judgment remains necessary" for safety-critical decisions (pqac-00000065).

**Frozen versus regenerated code.** No controlled randomized comparison exists, but indirect evidence favors freezing. ACE-CaP-0 achieved 92.1% with frozen programs and no agent during evaluation (pqac-00000016). WetRobo showed that reusing generated code reduced execution from 2 h 40 min to 3 min 27 s (pqac-00000002). RHO deploys single-turn frozen programs at test time (pqac-00000006). However, online revision can be "much more successful than one-shot execution in some settings, so freezing is not universally more reliable" (pqac-00000006). The practical recommendation is to freeze code once validated and implement regression testing when the library changes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010).

**Missing evidence.** Catch rates and false-alarm rates for most individual safeguard layers are unreported. No study systematically measures the precision and recall of human approval gates (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010).

## 3. Agent- or AI-Designed Physical Hardware for Laboratory Robots

**This is the area with the largest evidence gap.** No published study was found in which a language model or generative-AI system designed a laboratory fixture, holder, gripper, adapter, or docking feature that was then 3D-printed and tested on real laboratory robot hardware, with reported first-pass fit rates, iterations to success, or human edits needed.

The closest evidence comes from **text-to-CAD generation** systems evaluated computationally:

- **CADSmith** (Barkley et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) used five agents and two nested correction loops (inner for code errors, outer for geometric validation using OpenCASCADE measurements and VLM judgment). It achieved 100% execution rate on a 100-prompt benchmark and improved median IoU from 0.8085 to 0.9629 and reduced mean Chamfer Distance from 28.37 to 0.74 (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). Failure modes included "structurally incorrect yet geometrically valid solids" and subtle gaps missed by fixed viewing angles (pqac-00000015). No physical fabrication or testing was reported (pqac-00000012).

- **IterCAD** (Hu et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 0.64% invalid ratio (~99.36% code validity) and low median Chamfer distance of 0.10 on Text2CAD benchmarks (pqac-00000014). Its iterative multimodal correction averaged 2.34 turns per design. No physical validation was reported.

- **AgentsCAD** (George et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) specifically targeted design-for-manufacturing of FDM parts using multi-agent LLM reasoning, but was evaluated computationally.

**3D-printed laboratory components** are widely documented in the self-driving-lab literature. Doloi et al. (2025) reviewed advances in low-cost 3D printing for laboratory automation, including "automatic liquid handlers, robotic arms, automated" components. However, these designs were human-engineered rather than AI-generated.

**Implication for the BYU proposal.** The proposal to have an agent design connecting hardware (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers) would represent genuinely novel work. The closest precedent is CADSmith's computational CAD generation pipeline, which could be extended to lab-fixture design with physical validation. The expected workflow would involve: LLM generates CadQuery/OpenSCAD code → geometric validation loop → 3D printing → physical fit testing → iteration. Based on CADSmith's computational results, one might expect high code-execution rates but significant iteration for dimensional accuracy and functional fit, requiring human measurement feedback.

## 4. Provenance and Auditability for Agent-Operated Laboratories

### Demonstrated Approaches

**Git-based provenance.** WetRobo packages the robot's base stack, skill instructions (AGENTS.md), and agent-generated programs in a Git repository, with trial snapshots retained as branches. This creates a "record linking the starting software, agent-generated modifications, and individual attempts" (pqac-00000024). However, it does not include signed commits, immutable logs, or formal linkage from commits to measured physical outcomes (pqac-00000024).

**Hash-chained audit ledger.** La Agente Óptima implements the most rigorous provenance: "all robot state transitions pass through one funnel that atomically persists state and appends a line-delimited JSON entry to an append-only, hash-chained audit ledger. Each entry records the actor, action, structured payload, UTC timestamp, predecessor hash, and SHA-256 hashes of the complete state before and after the transition" (pqac-00000026). This enables reconstruction of "the requesting person, technician certification of the physical deck, autonomous actions between request and measurement, and whether the record was altered" (pqac-00000026).

**Community database deposition.** LabscriptAI deposits experimental data with metadata to FPBase (excitation/emission spectra, quantum yields) and EnzymeML (raw kinetics data), providing "traceability and reproducibility at the protocol/data level" (pqac-00000023).

**Digital-twin synchronization.** MATTERIX synchronizes the simulated and real robots via FoundationPose-based pose estimation, enabling comparison of predicted and actual outcomes (pqac-00000036). This provides a form of "what was planned versus what happened" comparison, though quantitative discrepancy metrics were not systematically reported.

### Cross-Site Reproducibility

WetRobo demonstrated cross-site reproducibility for cap removal across two laboratories with different grippers and camera placements; the coding-agent approach succeeded while a VLA baseline failed to transfer (pqac-00000024). LabscriptAI demonstrated cross-platform protocol translation with calibration CV below 5% across four liquid-handling platforms (pqac-00000052). These represent the strongest published demonstrations, though both involve limited task sets.

### Standards

**No retrieved publication specifically discusses ISO 10218:2025 or its cybersecurity clauses for networked robots in the context of agent-operated laboratories.** The 2025 revision of ISO 10218 (Parts 1 and 2) added requirements for cybersecurity of networked industrial robot systems, but the agent-lab literature has not yet engaged with these requirements. Cheng et al. (2026) call generally for "cybersecurity and AI-security practices" but name no specific standard (pqac-00000027). The proposed design principles—authenticated identity, state provenance, human certification, and tamper-evident audit trails (pqac-00000026)—align with the spirit of ISO 10218:2025 but have not been evaluated against its specific clauses.

## 5. Defensible Evaluation Design

Based on the surveyed literature, a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" should include the following elements:

### Outcome Metrics

Evaluations should report binary task success, quantitative partial progress through task-defined subgoals, safety violations, execution cost (model calls, tokens, GPU time, robot time), wall-clock time, and uncertainty intervals over repeated trials (pqac-00000056). Subgoals should be "implementation-independent, count repeated achievements only once, and specify whether an achieved state must remain satisfied" (pqac-00000056). For the fixture-design component, relevant metrics include code-execution success, geometric accuracy (IoU, Chamfer distance), first-pass physical fit rate, iterations to successful function, and human edits required (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

### Baselines

Comparisons should include at minimum three conditions: (1) a human expert designing the fixture and writing the workflow from scratch; (2) a scripted or deterministic workflow baseline using pre-existing fixtures; and (3) the agent system (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000063). CaP-X explicitly compared CaP-Agent0 against human-written programs and found the agent matched or exceeded humans on 4 of 7 tasks (pqac-00000019). VABAR uses "human-specified workflow or graph baselines" alongside agent results (pqac-00000058).

### Sample Sizes

Current practice varies widely: ACE-CaP-0 used 30 trials per task (240 total) (pqac-00000016); CaP-Bench used 25 hardware trials per task (pqac-00000056); VoxPoser used 5 real tasks with 10 trials each; BUMBLE used 70 trials across three buildings (pqac-00000057). The literature recommends that "sample sizes should be large enough to support uncertainty estimates rather than relying on single runs" and should use Wilson intervals or Bayesian methods (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000061). For the proposed evaluation, **≥25 trials per task per condition** would align with current best practice, with reporting of confidence intervals.

### Expected Failure Rates

The literature suggests the following baseline expectations:
- **Best manipulation systems (frozen code):** 83–100% per-task success, 92% aggregate (ACE-CaP-0) (pqac-00000016)
- **Code-as-policy with perturbations:** 12–26% under position/instruction perturbations (CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO) (pqac-00000018)
- **Chemistry laboratory manipulation:** 75–90% for pick-and-place and pouring (MATTERIX) (pqac-00000032)
- **Sim-to-real gap:** simulation screening catches many failures but typically 10–15% of simulated successes fail on real hardware (pqac-00000004)
- **Safety violations:** policies exceeding 90% task success were unsafe in 18–28% of episodes; 38–56% of successful rollouts in one benchmark violated a safety clause (pqac-00000005)

### Evaluation Architecture

A defensible benchmark should: (1) use sealed or independently verifiable judges, separating diagnostic feedback from final evaluation (pqac-00000056); (2) deliberately inject execution-layer and sample-identity faults, scoring detection, localization, safe abort, recovery, and provenance preservation (pqac-00000059); (3) audit evaluator errors against references and report false acceptances and rejections separately (pqac-00000060); (4) freeze or explicitly measure any learning during testing (pqac-00000061); (5) test both simulation and physical embodiments with paired trials (pqac-00000058); and (6) disclose all human involvement including setup, resets, and reward code (pqac-00000057).

### For the Specific BYU Proposal

An evaluation of "agent designs fixture + writes workflow + arm runs it" is unprecedented in the literature. The closest analogs combine CADSmith-style computational CAD validation with ACE-CaP-0-style physical execution testing. A defensible protocol would:

1. **Fixture design:** Agent generates CadQuery code for each connecting part → geometric validation (IoU, Chamfer) → 3D print → measure dimensional accuracy → test fit on robot → score first-pass success, iterations, and human edits.
2. **Workflow writing:** Agent generates motion/manipulation code → simulation dry run → physical execution with ≥25 trials → score task success, safety violations, and latency.
3. **End-to-end:** Score the fraction of parts that fit, workflows that execute, and complete alloy-development loops that run without human handling, compared against human-designed fixtures and human-written workflows under matched conditions.
4. **Provenance:** Log every agent session, generated artifact, commit, and physical outcome in a hash-chained audit trail, then verify that the full chain can be reconstructed.

The literature suggests one should expect 75–92% physical success rates for well-developed manipulation tasks, significant iteration (2–5 cycles) for first-pass fixture fit, and that human intervention will be necessary for physical setup, safety checks, and debugging hardware faults that agents cannot diagnose remotely (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000032).

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

- **Per-task monetary cost** is essentially unreported across all systems.
- **Human-intervention frequency** is rarely quantified.
- **False-alarm rates** for individual safeguard layers are almost never measured.
- **AI-designed physical lab hardware** fabricated and tested on real robots: **no published evidence exists.**
- **ISO 10218:2025 cybersecurity clauses** have not been analyzed in the agent-lab literature.
- **Controlled comparison of frozen versus regenerated code** has not been published.
- **End-to-end agent-designed-fixture-plus-workflow evaluation** has no published precedent.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports an evaluation of GPT-3-turbo and GPT-4 generating Python scripts for an Opentrons OT-2 liquid-handling robot, validated in simulation rather than executed on a physical robot. The system extracted scripts from LLM outputs, ran them with opentrons_simulate, sent error messages back to the model for correction, and repeated this loop for up to five iterations. For detailed, step-by-step cell-culture medium-exchange instructions, GPT-4 succeeded in 13 of 22 sessions on the first iteration (59%) and 21 of 22 after five iterations (95%); excluding sessions aborted because the LLM API was busy, the reported rate was 100%. For more ambiguous, goal-oriented instructions, GPT-4 succeeded in 3 of 17 sessions initially and 12 of 17 after five iterations (71%), or 92% excluding LLM-API-busy sessions. GPT-3-turbo achieved 50% after five iterations for step-by-step instructions and 17% for goal-oriented instructions. Reported failure modes were Opentrons/API or protocol errors, including ApiDeprecationError, ExceptionInProtocolError, and MalformedProtocolError, plus Python errors such as FileNotFoundError, IndentationError, NameError, RuntimeError, and SyntaxError; API-busy sessions were separately labeled. The excerpt provides no latency, monetary cost per task, physical-robot success rate, or human-intervention rate, and it contains no results for Coscientist, CLAIRify, WetRobo, MATTERIX, CRESt, LabscriptAI, ACE-CaP-0, AMP1, or SPINE.

CLAIRify translates natural-language instructions into structured XDL plans, which are then executed by a Franka robot through constrained task-and-motion planning (TAMP), perception, and manipulation skills. The study evaluates methods on 12 complex real-world tasks, using three platform instances with differences in scene background and hardware characteristics. Each task-method combination receives nine trials, with three trials per platform. Trials use free-form language instructions covering both single-skill pick-and-place and multi-stage subgoal sequencing. Controller errors terminate baseline and AMP1-without-recovery trials. AMP1 with recovery-from-error (RfE) can request recovery through the harness and continue after a successful recovery, within the remaining time budget. contexts.context: The excerpt describes several pre-execution and execution-time safeguards, but does not provide evidence for typed skill libraries, explicit workspace/force limits, or a direct comparison between frozen code and per-run regeneration. Static and formal checks include translating commands into temporal logic, rejecting unsatisfiable plans, synthesizing controllers that reconcile plans with safety rules, pruning unsafe actions, and verifying invariants, guards, and abort conditions with an SMT solver. In one reported result, RoboGuard reduced unsafe execution under worst-case jailbreaks from over 92% to below 3%; Lang2LTL grounded 52 commands, including 12 unsatisfiable ones, and aborted those executions. Simulation dry runs and digital-twin-like proxies screen programs before robot execution, although transfer is imperfect: ReSkill achieved 72/80 simulated successes versus 62/80 real successes, while another system reported 8/10 reconstructed-scene solutions transferring to the robot. Runtime or post-execution monitors include VLM judges and learned success detectors, but their reliability can be poor: a fixed VLM accepted 50.0% of remaining hover failures, and one learned verifier was wrong on 91% of 699 later rollouts. Human review is cited as able to catch model feedback errors, but no human-approval catch or false-alarm rate is measured. The only frozen-code evidence is ReSkill’s deployment of simulation-developed programs without regeneration.
contexts.question: What safeguards and verification layers catch agent errors before or during execution on robots? Include typed skill libraries, static checks, simulation dry runs, digital twin validation, workspace/force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates. What are measured catch rates and false-alarm rates? Is freezing agent-written code more reliable than regenerating each run?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a layered safety and verification architecture for robot-executed agent plans. An agent planner converts scientific intent into executable protocols that must pass pre-execution validation, execution-time safeguards, and post-execution auditing. These layers operate with a human governor and generate provenance logs and quality-control artifacts; anomaly feedback updates memory and future plans. The text also emphasizes independent verification and licensure, plus continuous change management and re-verification whenever models, tools, or hardware change. Relevant error-prevention mechanisms include constraint-aware planning with explicit unit and volume checks, retrieval from protocol and instrument documentation, preservation of reasoning and tool traces, and abstention or escalation when uncertainty is high. For physical execution, conservative low-level controllers should keep actions within validated safety envelopes, while richer telemetry and observability support detection of misplaced or mis-sealed plates, bubbles, clogs, volume inconsistencies, and instrument errors. Pressure traces or camera-based sensing are cited as examples of detecting anomalies that may otherwise remain hidden. The excerpt does not provide measured catch rates or false-alarm rates, nor does it compare frozen agent-written code with regenerating code on every run. It also does not specifically document typed skill libraries, static checking, simulation dry runs, or a quantified digital-twin validation protocol, although it mentions digital-twin resimulation as a potentially time-consuming intervention.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several safeguards, but not the complete set listed in the question. Typed or structured skill-library checks are represented by Teach and Grow, which evaluates each skill block for scope, executor compatibility, outcome tests, recovery behavior, and provenance. VASO adds a static/formal layer by model-checking induced plans against temporal-logic safety specifications, achieving 96.8% specification compliance with an automatically generated state-to-proposition mapping and 97.2% with a handcrafted mapping; the guarantee depends on that mapping being correct. Acceptance and regression tests are important: removing RoboBridge’s validation reduced success from 83% to 69% and from 94% to 63% on two splits, while Skill2Real’s Governor and Verifier ablations also caused substantial drops. Statistical paired tests can be more permissive than Hoeffding tests: one Hoeffding test admitted no updates, whereas a paired test admitted 229 of 256 with no observed violations, though this is not a measured false-alarm rate. Checks can still miss broad regressions: a microwave routine passed its paired test but later caused 79 lost successes. The excerpt gives no direct evidence on workspace/force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates, digital twins, or catch/false-alarm rates. It also does not establish that freezing agent-written code is more reliable; it only reports frozen models/memory and identical deterministic rollouts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several verification and monitoring layers, but does not cover every safeguard named in the question. NeSyRo performs static and semantic checks by validating generated code with an SMT solver, testing skill preconditions with a PDDL planner, and generating probe code when observations are missing. This is presented as improving real-robot performance: on a partially observable Franka setup it reports 57.5% average success versus 10.6% for Code as Policies, with seven irreversible actions versus 53. Runtime monitoring is illustrated by Code-as-Monitor, which generates a VLM-based checker for spatio-temporal constraints and triggers replanning only when a violation is detected; in simulated block stacking it achieves 88.33% success versus 76.67% for a continuously queried baseline, while also reducing time. The excerpt gives no explicit catch-rate or false-alarm-rate measurements; success rates and irreversible-action counts are the main reported proxies. It suggests that freezing code after offline development can reduce runtime model errors and cost: RHO deploys a single-turn frozen program, while Embodied Turing Machines use code alone at test time. However, online revision can be much more successful than one-shot execution in some settings, so freezing is not universally more reliable. Typed skill libraries, human approval gates, digital-twin validation, explicit workspace/force limits, and detailed false-alarm statistics are not reported in this excerpt.
