contexts.context: The excerpt reports simulation- and benchmark-level results for CADSmith, not physical-hardware validation. CADSmith uses five agents and two nested correction loops: an inner loop for code execution errors and an outer loop using OpenCASCADE measurements and independent visual judgment. On a custom benchmark of 100 prompts across three difficulty tiers, it reached a 100% execution rate, compared with 95% for a zero-shot baseline. It also improved median F1 from 0.9707 to 0.9846, median IoU from 0.8085 to 0.9629, and reduced mean Chamfer Distance from 28.37 to 0.74. The excerpt characterizes prior systems differently: Query2CAD used iterative visual feedback but lacked geometric precision, while Text-to-CadQuery generated code in a single pass without iterative correction or specification validation. No information is provided here about 3D-printing, real-hardware testing, fixtures, holders, grippers, adapters, docking features, first-pass fit rates, iterations required to achieve fit, or the amount of human editing. The reported execution rate should therefore not be interpreted as a physical fit or manufacturing success rate.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports CADSmith results for programmatic text-to-CAD generation, but it does not provide evidence about 3D-printed parts tested on real hardware, first-pass physical fit rates, human edits, or the number of iterations to successful physical fit. For generated CAD execution, the full multi-agent pipeline achieved 100% execution success and reduced mean Chamfer Distance 38× versus zero-shot generation. By tier, T1 primitives achieved median F1 0.9985 and median IoU 0.9834; T2 engineering parts achieved median F1 0.9979 and median IoU 0.7661; and T3 complex parts achieved median F1 0.8859 and median IoU 0.9582. The strongest improvements occurred when iterative kernel-based feedback corrected fundamentally wrong but executable zero-shot geometry. Vision was especially important for complex parts: removing the rendered image increased T3 mean Chamfer Distance from 1.42 to 49.68 and reduced mean F1 from 0.85 to 0.74. Reported failure modes include structurally incorrect yet geometrically valid solids, construction approaches that diverge from the reference, and near-miss gaps that evade both kernel metrics and visual inspection. One T3 quadcopter-frame example converged on the first iteration but still contained subtle gaps. The excerpt does not quantify human intervention or physical-manufacturing success.

CADSmith appears only in the references. It does provide related evidence about CAD-agent performance on the 50-case Hephaestus-CCX benchmark, where generated STEP artifacts were evaluated with CalculiX finite-element analysis and typed engineering checkers. A single FEA-feedback round changed mean requirement pass by −1.3 to +30.9 percentage points across experimental settings, with an average gain of 13.4 points. In the longest GPT-5.5/high feedback loop, performance increased from 38.8% to 60.5% mean requirement pass, yielding 9 of 50 strict-passing artifacts, at 68 minutes per item. Reported failure and repair modes included structural underperformance requiring bracing or stiffness changes; mesh-sensitive or overly complex geometry; checker-contract problems such as missing metric aliases, mass fields, or selector bindings; and hidden mass-property errors that were not visually apparent. These are simulated engineering-validation outcomes rather than physical fit or hardware-test results, so they cannot establish first-pass assembly fit, real-world iteration counts, or human intervention requirements.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes LLM4CAD, a text- and multimodal-to-CAD approach in which GPT-4 and GPT-4V generate CAD programs that are compiled into 3D CAD models. The authors created a dataset covering shafts, nuts, flanges, springs, and gears, with textual descriptions, sketches, images, and 3D CAD models. A debugger was introduced to correct syntax errors in generated CAD programs and improve the rate at which those programs translate into 3D CAD models. The reported qualitative findings are that GPT-4 and GPT-4V show potential, particularly with the debugger, but continue to struggle with complex geometries. For GPT-4V, text-only input performed better on average than multimodal combinations in the reported Cap 1 and Cap 2 evaluations. contexts.context: The excerpt reports benchmark results for CaP-Agent0, the agent evaluated within the CaP-X framework, rather than separately identifying results for AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, or SPINE. On CaP-Bench, combining visual differencing, a synthesized skill library, and parallel reasoning substantially improves performance over the single-turn S3 baseline; CaP-Agent0 matches or exceeds human-written programs on 4 of 7 tasks. On LIBERO-PRO, its average success rates under initial-position (Pos) and instruction (Task) perturbations are: libero-object 0.22 and 0.18, libero-goal 0.26 and 0.17, and libero-spatial 0.12 and 0.14. Competing OpenVLA and π0 score 0.00 throughout, while π0.5 reaches 0.17/0.01, 0.38/0.00, and 0.20/0.01 respectively. On BEHAVIOR, Pick up Radio navigation/task success is 80%/56% for CaP-Agent0 versus 72%/24% for S3 and 88%/36% for humans; Pick up Soda Can is 84%/72% versus 52%/32% and 80%/72%. The excerpt also describes CaP-Gym’s real-robot interface and zero-shot demonstrations. It reports no latency-per-task or human-intervention metrics, and provides no results for AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, or SPINE.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports only CaP-Agent0 results on the LIBERO-PRO robot-manipulation benchmark; it does not provide results for CaP-Gym, AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, or SPINE, nor does it report latency per task or human-intervention metrics. LIBERO-PRO evaluates generalization under initial-position perturbations (Pos) and instruction perturbations (Task), with 50 trials per task. CaP-Agent0’s average success rates are: libero-object, 0.218 (Pos) and 0.182 (Task); libero-goal, 0.256 (Pos) and 0.168 (Task); and libero-spatial, 0.118 (Pos) and 0.140 (Task). The reported failure modes include perception errors, grasp-generation failures, and control-API failures. A specific perception issue is that SAM 3 may segment a tomato sauce can when asked for an alphabet soup can. Occluded scenes and non-top-down camera views produce angled grasps, while the absence of collision-aware motion planning can cause other objects to be knocked over, preventing secure grasping. The excerpt’s cube-stack analysis states that strong models often succeed on the first try and use later turns for recovery, but it supplies no latency or human-intervention figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports results only for ACE-CaP-0; it contains no results for CaP-X, CaP-Gym, AMP1, or SPINE, and therefore provides no cross-system comparison or failure-mode breakdown for those methods. ACE-CaP-0 was evaluated on eight real-world manipulation tasks, with 30 trials per task (240 total), using frozen programs and no human or coding agent during evaluation. Its overall success rate was 92.1% (221/240). Task-level success rates were: Charger Insertion 100.0% (30/30), Bread Packing 83.3% (25/30), Bottle Uncapping 90.0% (27/30), Cup Nesting 93.3% (28/30), Flower Insertion 90.0% (27/30), Chicken Plating 96.7% (29/30), Parcel Reorientation 93.3% (28/30), and Shoe Packing 90.0% (27/30). The excerpt does not identify qualitative failure modes; failures are only represented by unsuccessful trial counts. Mean physical execution latency per task was 1.65, 1.93, 2.23, 1.58, 1.37, 1.12, 0.97, and 2.27 minutes, respectively. Human involvement was limited during development to at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task; resets for collecting demonstrations were excluded. No human intervention occurred during evaluation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a layered provenance and auditability approach for agent-operated laboratories, but it does not explicitly specify a complete chain linking an agent request to generated code or CAD, a version-control commit, and the final physical outcome. The proposed architecture has an agent planner compile scientific intent into executable protocols, followed by three controls: pre-execution validation, execution-time safeguards, and post-execution auditing. These controls interact with a human governor and generate provenance logs and QC artifacts, while anomaly feedback updates memory and future plans. The infrastructure layer contributes standard device interfaces, telemetry, and state monitoring. The text also calls for external memory connected to run histories and reagent lifetimes, preservation of reasoning and tool traces, and continuous verification of what was executed, observed, and scientifically interpretable. Independent verification, licensure, continuous change management, and re-verification after model, tool, or hardware updates are identified as deployment requirements. The excerpt discusses the need to detect, attribute, recover, and compare failures, including silent biological and execution errors. However, it reports no demonstrated cross-site reproducibility results, nor does it describe specific request/code/CAD-to-commit identity schemes, cryptographic provenance, or software repository practices. ISO 10218:2025 and cybersecurity standards for networked robots are not mentioned in the supplied pages.
contexts.question: What provenance and auditability methods link the agent request, generated code or CAD, the commit, and the physical outcome in agent-operated laboratories? What reproducibility across sites has been demonstrated? What relevant standards (ISO 10218:2025, cybersecurity for networked robots) exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several provenance and auditability mechanisms, but not a complete end-to-end chain linking the original agent request, generated code or CAD, a version-control commit, and the physical result. Natural-language task delegation leads to agent-generated programs, which are preserved as exemplar branches. Action records and saved trial RGB-D data provide an execution trail: programs can be rerun against saved sensor data, and recorded actions are used to update AGENTS.md with reusable installation-specific rules. This supports traceability from evolved behavior to observations and subsequent procedural knowledge, although the excerpt does not explicitly mention commit hashes, immutable logs, CAD provenance, dataset identifiers, cryptographic signing, or hardware safety/cybersecurity audit records. Demonstrated cross-site reproducibility concerns the cap-removal task: the coding agent succeeded in both Lab X and Lab Y despite different grippers and camera placements. Reuse of generated camera and motion code also shortened repeat execution in the same setting. The evidence is limited because trials involved one agent/model and individual adaptation sequences rather than repeated independent adaptations. ISO 10218:2025 and cybersecurity standards for networked robots are not discussed in this excerpt, so no claims about their requirements or compliance can be supported here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a provenance and auditability architecture for an agent-operated laboratory bridge. Remote callers authenticate with individually issued HTTPS API keys, allowing actions to be attributed to a person rather than merely to a service. Technician setup is certified locally at the robot bench, while autonomous bridge actions receive a distinct system identity. All robot state transitions pass through one funnel that atomically persists state and appends a line-delimited JSON entry to an append-only, hash-chained audit ledger. Each entry records the actor, action, structured payload, UTC timestamp, predecessor hash, and SHA-256 hashes of the complete state before and after the transition. This makes tampering detectable and permits independent verification of the first broken ledger entry. The ledger can reconstruct the requesting person, technician certification of the physical deck, autonomous actions between request and measurement, and whether the record was altered. The excerpt does not describe explicit linkage among an agent request, generated code or CAD artifacts, source-control commits, and final physical outcomes; nor does it report demonstrated cross-site reproducibility. It also contains no discussion of ISO 10218:2025 or cybersecurity standards for networked robots. Thus, it supports claims about authenticated identity, state provenance, human certification, and tamper-evident robot audit trails, but not the broader standards or reproducibility questions.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that LabSafety Bench reveals a substantial gap between LLM performance on structured laboratory-safety questions and realistic scenario-based safety reasoning. DeepSeek-R1 is identified as the most robust overall model, ranking among the top two on both text-only multiple-choice questions and scenario-based questions. However, no evaluated model exceeded 70% accuracy on hazard identification in realistic scenarios, and the results are described as unreliable for safety-critical deployment. The excerpt emphasizes a pronounced difference between identifying simple hazards and analyzing complex operational risks, including improper operation and the most likely safety incidents. It therefore indicates that the safety threshold was not met by current top-performing models; the only explicit numerical benchmark in this excerpt is the 70% hazard-identification ceiling. The supplied pages do not provide model-by-model numerical scores for either hazard identification or consequence identification. They mention that ChemCrow showed a slight improvement on scenario-based questions, particularly the Consequence Identification Test, but do not state its score or the scores of other models on that test. Overall, the findings support rigorous human oversight and independent verification before laboratory deployment.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that LabSafety Bench evaluated eight proprietary models, seven open-weight LLMs, and four open-weight vision-language models. The benchmark contained 765 laboratory-safety multiple-choice questions and 404 realistic laboratory scenarios. DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o achieved the highest overall performance, although no model was flawless. LLMs performed substantially worse on complex scenario-based tasks than on simpler knowledge-oriented questions, revealing weak adaptability, inappropriate risk prioritization, and hallucinations. In particular, no model exceeded 70% accuracy on the Hazards Identification Test. The excerpt does not provide the exact numerical scores for individual models on the Hazards Identification or Consequence Identification tests, nor does it state the benchmark’s safety threshold. It also indicates that supervised fine-tuning substantially improved smaller models, while specialized agents such as ChemCrow produced inconsistent gains and standard RAG often reduced performance. The authors therefore recommend using high-performing models with continuous human oversight rather than treating any model as fully reliable for laboratory safety decisions. Exact per-model hazard-identification scores, consequence-identification scores, and the formal safety-threshold definition would need to be obtained from the paper’s figures, tables, or later results sections.

contexts.context: MATTERIX is presented as a multi-scale digital-twin framework for chemistry laboratories, combining physical robot manipulation with heat-transfer and chemical-kinetics simulation. Its digital-twin features include an integrated semantics engine, hierarchical workflow representation, extensive libraries of laboratory assets and manipulation skills, and perception tools for constructing laboratory environments and workflows. The system synchronizes a simulated robot with the real robot: FoundationPose estimates object locations from the observed physical scene, updates the digital twin, and enables the real robot to follow simulated motions. In validation experiments, object pick-and-place achieved 75% success across 12 trials (9 successful attempts), with failures attributed to pose estimation, calibration, action, object-frame, and digital-to-real asset mismatches. Liquid pouring achieved 90% success in 10 real experiments; the main failure involved inaccurate beaker pose estimation. For liquid-station setup, a simulated hierarchical state-machine policy using inverse kinematics and low-level controllers was transferred zero-shot to the FR3 robot and OT-2 liquid handler. Thus, workflows and policies are developed and refined in simulation before being executed physically, supporting sim-to-real testing while exposing discrepancies such as differing liquid behavior, vessel dimensions, and workspace geometry. Current limitations include approximate reaction models, lack of gas-phase simulation, and difficulty planning long-horizon workflows.
contexts.question: What are the specific results, success rates, and digital twin features of MATTERIX for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratory automation? How does MATTERIX validate plans in simulation before physical execution?

Its reported capabilities include multi-scale data simulation, physics-based and photorealistic simulation, particle simulation, robot-learning libraries, sensor simulation, semantic modelling, domain-specific assets, real-world demonstration, workflow verification, orchestration and scheduling, task and workflow planning, and robot navigation. MATTERIX supports multiple heterogeneous robots, including fixed-base and mobile manipulators, and enables long-horizon laboratory tasks and workflows. A full simulated chemistry laboratory modeled after an Acceleration Consortium self-driving lab includes fume hoods, liquid-handling, solid-dispensing, glove-box, washing/drying stations, and several robotic systems. Objects and workstations are represented using Universal Scene Description (USD), with physical, visual, hierarchical, transformation, material, and metadata properties. Fluids and powders can be initialized with specified quantities and locations and simulated through GPU-accelerated position-based dynamics. For planning and validation, reusable manipulation and perception skills are organized hierarchically into workflows, allowing tasks to be composed and executed in simulation; the feature comparison explicitly identifies workflow verification, although the excerpt does not explain its exact algorithm or report plan-validation success rates before physical execution.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX as an open-source, GPU-based digital-twin platform for robotics-assisted chemistry automation. Its features include physics-based, particle and multi-scale simulation; photorealistic digital assets; a semantics engine; robot-learning and skill libraries; computer vision; classical and learning-based motion planning; obstacle avoidance; hierarchical state-machine workflows; and integration with multiple robots and automated platforms. Users can construct new environments by specifying laboratory assets and poses, use CAD, 3D scanning, or NeRF reconstruction, and model equipment such as robot arms, mobile manipulators, liquid handlers, glassware, and instruments. MATTERIX supports long-horizon, contact-rich, multi-step organic and inorganic chemistry workflows and sim-to-real deployment. Before physical execution, a human or large language model generates a workflow, which MATTERIX executes in the digital twin using reusable skills and planners. It checks whether the proposed sequence produces the target chemical through a database of known reactions and approximate chemical kinetics, while simulated perception and robot control test the workflow. The real environment is then matched to simulation using camera-based object-pose perception and robot alignment. The excerpt reports demonstrations of two multi-step workflows and deployment in a real laboratory, but it does not provide numerical success rates or detailed per-task performance percentages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX as a multi-scale, GPU-accelerated simulation framework for creating high-fidelity digital twins of chemistry laboratories. Its modeled capabilities include robotic physical manipulation, powder and liquid dynamics, device functionality, heat transfer, basic chemical reaction kinetics, logical processes, and continuous behaviors. The framework combines realistic physics simulation, photorealistic rendering, and a modular GPU-accelerated semantics engine. It also provides open-source asset libraries and interfaces, hierarchical plan definitions, and a modular skill library that can incorporate learning-based methods. Built on Nvidia Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, MATTERIX supports fast parallel GPU simulation, contact-rich interactions, precise collision detection, object-definition APIs, and robot-learning libraries. Plans and workflows can be designed, tested, and iterated in the virtual laboratory before deployment, allowing robotic actions, environmental conditions, sensor integration, and experimental protocols to be evaluated safely and efficiently. This simulation-first process reduces dependence on costly physical trials, supports synthetic-data generation, and enables sim-to-real transfer to robotic chemistry setups. However, the supplied pages do not report specific numerical results, task success rates, validation percentages, or detailed experimental benchmarks; they only state that sim-to-real transfer was demonstrated and that hypothetical automated workflows can be tested in silico.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX as a digital twin for chemistry laboratories that combines a physics engine with a modular semantics engine. Its features include FoundationPose-based model-free 6D object pose estimation and tracking, USD 3D asset models, robot manipulation, liquid handling, device functionality simulation, heat transfer, and first-order chemical kinetics. The semantics engine supports behaviors such as OT-2 tip loading/removal, aspiration and dispensing, heater operation, and a mobile robot turning a faucet knob. GPU parallelization produced only 2.97% and 3.42% overhead for 2048 and 4096 parallel environments, respectively, when heat-transfer semantics were enabled. MATTERIX simulates multi-step workflows using a hierarchical state machine, combining manipulation and particle dynamics with thermal and reaction models. Plans are validated in simulation by enforcing user-defined preconditions—such as nonzero reactant concentrations and permissible temperature ranges—before reactions proceed, and by modeling specified reaction-rate parameters. Simulated experiments are compared with real measurements, including mass changes and camera-based color signals. The excerpt reports faster simulated reaction progress than the physical experiment, motivating online parameter adaptation. It also identifies three real-world evaluations: object pick-and-place, liquid handling, and a long-horizon sample-preparation experiment. Specific overall task success rates are not provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX as a digital-twin-based framework for robotics-assisted chemistry automation, but it does not provide specific experimental success rates, benchmark results, or numerical performance figures. Its digital-twin features include simulated chemical workflows that track compound identity and concentration in containers, enforce reaction preconditions such as temperature and reactant presence, and apply approximate concentration updates after reactions. These estimates are explicitly qualitative rather than quantitatively accurate, since the simulator supports only forward reactions represented with SMARTS templates and uses semi-quantitative verification rather than detailed kinetics or quantum chemistry. MATTERIX generates plans through a hierarchical task-definition framework and a GPU-parallelizable skill library combining classical motion planning and learning-based policies. The workflow is validated before physical execution by checking preconditions, simulating robotic manipulations and reactions, and comparing the resulting simulated chemical states with expected outcomes. This provides feedback for autonomous-agent training and helps chemists debug feasibility, logical flow, errors, and inefficiencies in experimental plans. The broader execution stack includes collision-free cuRobo motion planning, PPO reinforcement learning with curriculum scheduling, and FoundationPose object-pose estimation using available CAD models, although the excerpt does not report their task-level success rates.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents several MATTERIX capabilities relevant to robotics-assisted chemistry automation, but it does not provide explicit numerical success rates or overall plan-validation percentages. MATTERIX supports hierarchical state machines for multi-scale chemistry simulations and experimentally demonstrated workflows involving heater control, robot motion, liquid pouring, mixing, and reduction–oxidation chemistry. Robot trajectories are computed using inverse kinematics. Its digital-twin thermal model represents heat transfer among the heater, beaker, solution, and ambient environment through energy-balance equations, while also using Biot, Rayleigh, Grashof, and Prandtl numbers to characterize conduction and convection. A reported organic-chemistry deployment used a plate-heater target of 40°C; the solution stayed near 35°C, producing a relatively slow reaction rate. The physics and semantics engines provide the simulation workflow: at every simulation step, current physical states and actions are passed to the physics engine to calculate the next physical state, after which semantic processes are iterated. This architecture supports checking simulated robot and chemistry behavior before deployment, although the excerpt does not spell out a separate pass/fail planning metric. The cited deployment section also points to videos of real-world validation using Franka robots and an Opentrons liquid handler.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX as a digital-twin platform for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratories that combines configurable virtual workstations, reusable assets, hierarchical skills, workflows, physics simulation, and a semantics engine. Users define workstation assets and types in a configuration dictionary, allowing MATTERIX to generate virtual environments ranging from simple policy-training setups to realistic multi-equipment laboratories for feasibility studies, layout optimization, and monitoring. Skills are organized hierarchically: primitive actions such as joint control, inverse-kinematics planning, grasping, whole-body control, Cartesian motion, waiting, cuRobo obstacle-aware planning, and policy checkpoints can be combined into abstract operations such as pick-and-place. Chemists specify the actual objects while roboticists develop the reusable skill library. The integrated semantics engine supplements physical state with logical and continuous semantic states, enabling behaviors such as liquid aspiration, pipette synchronization, heater activation, heat transfer, and first-order chemical kinetics that are difficult to represent with conventional physics alone. Workflows advance through state-machine actions and are considered complete when all actions succeed. Simulation therefore provides a pre-execution validation mechanism: plans can be tested in virtual environments, checked for feasible sequential actions and semantic conditions, and evaluated before deployment to physical robots. This excerpt does not report numerical task success rates; it only describes capabilities and examples.
contexts.question: What are the specific results, success rates, and digital twin features of MATTERIX for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratory automation? How does MATTERIX validate plans in simulation before physical execution?

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that SPINE was evaluated on AgileX PiPER, a ROS Noetic and CAN-based bimanual system with four PiPER 6-DOF arms, USB-to-CAN adapters, and RealSense cameras. It compares a novice using SPINE with human operators using Claude Code across the same software, hardware, and hybrid fault cases. SPINE’s debugging approach combines a robot profile created from the known-good system, focused evidence gathering, diagnosis, software repair, physical intervention instructions, and revalidation. Successful recovery requires more than launching processes: follower arms and grippers must respond to master-arm commands and required camera streams must remain available. Its persistent-state mechanism includes profile data, closeout records containing symptoms, repairs, diagnoses, corrective actions, and validation evidence, plus incident memory for future investigations. The completion gate only permits closure when the latest validation results pass after the most recent intervention; unresolved records retain their diagnosis and blocker. This bridges the cyber-physical gap by treating configuration and code faults together with disconnected cables, cameras, CAN links, and safety controls, while requiring fresh physical observations and validation. contexts.context: For the AgileX PiPER arm, SPINE increased mean fault resolution from 99% to 100% and reduced mean time-to-teleoperation by 38% compared with human operators using Claude Code without SPINE’s structured workflow. Its debugging approach is an iterative observe–triage–repair–validation loop. Triage dispatches four read-only diagnostic sub-agents in parallel, combines their reports into a fixability decision, and then separates repair into either a software edit or a physical operator action. Verification reruns the live teleoperation pipeline and hidden readiness checks; unresolved cases return to triage with new evidence, and a case closes only when the full pipeline and readiness checks pass in the same cycle. SPINE’s persistent-state mechanism is a robot-specific profile built from documentation, known-good repositories, setup facts, and operator-confirmed information. The profile stores requirements, troubleshooting procedures, validation criteria, source contracts, live probes, hidden checks, and physical playbooks. Incident outcomes and validation evidence are retained for later sessions. This bridges the cyber-physical gap by combining software inspection and repair with live device, middleware, connectivity, controller, cable, and hardware evidence, plus guided operator interventions. Thus, it targets pre-operational failures that prevent perception, middleware bringup, or teleoperation before a usable robot action interface exists.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes SPINE’s architecture and debugging method but does not provide the PiPER-arm experimental results or a numerical success rate; the visible table only begins listing injected DOBOT and PiPER scenarios. SPINE uses two skills: profile building creates robot-specific context, while debugging combines that profile with live evidence, incident memory, and operator observations. Its debugger follows an observe–triage–repair–verify loop. Specialist agents diagnose terminal evidence, software/configuration deviations, hardware visibility, and readiness relevance in parallel; the backend aggregates evidence, maintains a blocker ledger, and selects the next intervention. Software repairs are followed by after-fix validation, while physical interventions are selected from hardware playbooks and confirmed through operator responses, probes, or manual observations. Closure requires complete execution of the confirmed teleoperation command graph, hidden readiness checks, and successful validation—not merely an LLM diagnosis. Persistent state is maintained through the compiled robot profile, per-robot memory, incident history, blocker-ledger updates, and persistent step history. The cyber-physical gap is bridged by combining executable software checks with live observations of cables, device enumeration, bus connectivity, controller readiness, and operator-guided hardware actions, then requiring end-to-end teleoperation readiness after the latest intervention.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not mention LabscriptAI, a 96.7% simulation-pass rate, a 90-task liquid-handling benchmark, or comparisons with commercial baselines. It instead describes a dual-agent framework for translating natural-language laboratory protocols into robotic commands. The Validation Agent checks three dimensions: completeness, parameter accuracy, and execution order. The stated error categories include parsing failures, parameter conversion errors, and execution-order inconsistencies; examples include omitted dispensing or washing steps, incorrect conversion of volumes, durations, or temperatures, and invalid sequencing such as liquid handling before tip attachment. Detected errors are returned as structured feedback identifying the error type, location, and correction guidance, triggering iterative regeneration. The evaluation used 30 protocols selected from 1,000 web-collected ELISA protocols, with separate ground truths for structured protocols and device-level command sequences. Seven parser models were tested, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 was the default heterogeneous validator; GPT-5 and Llama-4-Maverick were comparative validators. Each protocol received up to three attempts, with failures after the third attempt classified as Final Fail.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specify concrete evaluation metrics, sample sizes, acceptable failure rates, or a prescribed benchmark for agent-driven robotic fixture-and-workflow writing. It does, however, provide a defensible high-level evaluation framework. Evaluation should progress from core knowledge and reasoning to task completion, interactive performance, and ultimately real-world laboratory outcomes. Task-oriented benchmarks should test complete end-to-end workflows rather than isolated question answering. Interactive evaluation should score the full process—including interaction, decision-making, and adaptation—not merely the final result. For robotic workflows, the strongest evidence would therefore come from execution on physical laboratory hardware, ideally in a Self-Driving Laboratory setting, with outcomes grounded in actual experiments. Comparisons should include human expert judgments and strong scripted or conventional workflow baselines, since the excerpt notes that human or LLM judges are often needed when quantitative metrics are unavailable or insufficient. The text also cautions that external tool use is not automatically beneficial, so ablations comparing agent-only, tool-augmented, and scripted systems would be appropriate. Finally, evaluation should account for reliability, hallucination, logical reasoning failures, data contamination, safety, and practical feasibility: an experimentally plausible plan may still be physically infeasible, and biomedical agents require governance emphasizing truthfulness, robustness, fairness, resilience, and privacy.

A defensible benchmark should use hidden or independently verifiable tests where possible, clearly document judge access and error, and separate diagnostic feedback from final evaluation. contexts.context: The excerpt argues that agent-driven robotic workflows need evaluation protocols that make interfaces and system components explicit, because terminal task success is currently difficult to compare across methods. A defensible benchmark should report the robot interface, observations, planner, controller, and opportunities for correction, while testing not only task completion but also execution feedback, memory, replanning, transfer, and behavior over long deployments. Existing physical studies are small—VoxPoser used five real tasks with ten trials each, while BUMBLE used 70 trials across three buildings—so these figures illustrate current practice rather than an established sample-size standard or expected failure rate. The survey identifies no shared benchmark and emphasizes that self-improvement evaluations should measure capability as experience accumulates. They should include regression tests on earlier capabilities, held-out tasks or configurations for transfer, and comparisons under matched FM, wall-clock, and interaction budgets. Human involvement must be disclosed because evaluators, prompts, setup, resets, and reward code frequently depend on designers; HARBOR is noted as the only comparison with fixed-procedure loops under the same budget, although it received human heuristics unavailable to baselines. The excerpt does not prescribe specific metrics, failure-rate targets, or a formal human-expert benchmark, but it supports reporting success, reliability over repeated trials, transfer, regression performance, and supervision requirements alongside scripted and human comparisons.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a layered evaluation design for agent-driven scientific or robotic workflows. First, task-oriented evaluation should measure complete end-to-end success with quantitative metrics appropriate to the workflow: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, hit rate, tool-use accuracy, unit-test pass rate, and—where physical experiments are involved—yield, purity, reaction mass efficiency, space-time yield, and E-factor. Second, interactive benchmarks should evaluate the full process rather than only the final result, including planning, tool/API interaction, decision-making, adaptation over time, memory or internal state, stopping decisions, and improvement across iterative trials. The strongest validation is real-world execution, such as wet-lab or self-driving-laboratory experiments, with outcomes tied to scientific objectives. A defensible benchmark should therefore include standardized, realistic tasks, reproducible protocols or fixtures, held-out cases, and both automated and expert review. Baselines should include a scripted or conventional workflow, the agent, and human experts; the excerpt specifically describes comparisons against expert protocols, human trainees, senior experts, and GPT-4. Human qualitative assessment remains important for scientific soundness, practical utility, and interpretability, while LLM judges can improve scalability when calibrated against human ratings. The excerpt does not specify recommended sample sizes or expected failure rates, so those must be established empirically through pilot power analysis, repeated runs, confidence intervals, and transparent failure categorization.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a defensible benchmark built around more than aggregate success. It should use executable or sealed judges, report success and failure categories, and record agent claims separately from verified outcomes. Useful metrics include success rate, overclaiming and underclaiming, Python or execution errors, infeasible actions, task-completion errors, cost, model calls, interaction budgets, and median wall time. Results should include variation across multiple runs or seeds; SEAR reports spread over three runs, while RoboDojo requires three simulation seeds and all three real embodiments. Sample sizes should be explicit and broad enough to expose generalization: RobotWorld covers 84 tasks, Embodied First Exam uses 1,156 tasks across 35 suites, RoboARCade evaluates 22 long-horizon tasks, and VABAR uses 30 generated instances per condition. Controls should isolate effects of repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged information, budget, and luck. A strong workflow benchmark should vary interface and feedback conditions, include hidden-layout or held-out validation checks, and test both simulation and physical embodiments. Comparisons should include human-specified workflow or graph baselines, as VABAR does, alongside agent results; the excerpt does not provide a detailed human-expert protocol or scripted-baseline design.

contexts.context: A defensible benchmark for agent-driven robotic workflows should report more than task success. It should specify the evaluator’s visibility, costs, variance, token/dollar/time budgets, seeds, interfaces, perturbation splits, and whether paired real-robot trials exist and how many. Simulation-only results should be linked to hardware through paired trials and uncertainty intervals; when simulation–reality correlation is weak, additional simulated rollouts may not improve precision. Evaluation should estimate judge quality using an independent reference check: sample accepted episodes, state the sample size, report the proportion of accepted episodes that are actually unsuccessful (one minus judge precision), and provide uncertainty intervals. False positives and false negatives should be reported separately, including false acceptance under agent search. Baselines should include manual expert annotation/resetting and deterministic or scripted evaluators, with matched conditions and budgets; HALTER illustrates reporting agreement with manual labels and operator interventions. For workflow or code-writing agents, benchmarks should rerun earlier task–seed pairs after library updates and report skill-library retention alongside gains on new tasks. Comparisons should use repeated paired evaluations for stochastic agents, fixed seeds, matched interfaces, and explicit sample sizes. The excerpt does not prescribe a universal expected failure-rate threshold; it instead requires measuring and auditing failures among accepted episodes rather than assuming benchmark success is reliable.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies benchmark properties that are relevant to a defensible evaluation of agent-driven robotic workflows, but it does not specify recommended numerical sample sizes, expected failure rates, or a complete human-expert comparison protocol. Evaluation should distinguish task-level planning from motion-level execution and should expose more than terminal success: execution history, failures, outcome evidence, goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, transition/precondition errors, and the way observations are returned to the agent. Feedback-rich benchmarks such as LoHoRavens and LongAct are especially suitable for evaluating adaptation, diagnosis, and replanning. LongAct is notable because it includes an improvement-rate metric measuring gains from accumulated experience, which can support evaluation of continual self-improvement. EAI offers standardized symbolic interfaces and fine-grained planning and precondition-error analysis. EmbodiedBench provides broad coverage—1,128 vision-driven household reasoning, navigation, and manipulation tasks—useful for testing generalization across capabilities. RoboFail should be treated as a verification-oriented substrate rather than a benchmark of behavior generation. A rigorous study would therefore report success and failure by task and failure mode, execution/recovery behavior, adaptation gains, and performance against scripted and expert references, while clearly separating within-trial recovery from cross-trial or persistent improvement. The table itself does not establish effect sizes, repetitions, confidence intervals, or target failure-rate thresholds.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a defensible evaluation protocol that reports task success and failure modes together with the number of trials per condition, confidence or Bayesian intervals, and exactly what was repeated or resampled. Comparisons should use matched test states, verify the provenance of initial conditions, interleave policy rollouts blindly, and apply paired statistical tests with multiple-testing corrections; sequential or Bayesian methods are preferable to repeatedly checking naive tests. contexts.question:
Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab). Most remote work is done by AI coding agents: a GitHub comment starts an agent session in CI, which reaches a lab Raspberry Pi over SSH and drives the instrument (a gantry liquid handler, 3D printers, an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with Raspberry Pi cameras and AprilTags); risky actions such as starting a print wait for a human approval, and every session, command and result is recorded in the repository. The lab ran about 575 agent sessions in 30 days across seven repositories. A recent proposal of ours asks whether a language-model agent can design and validate the connecting hardware of an automated alloy-development loop (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers and fixtures, 3D-printed) and write the robot workflows around it, well enough that the loop runs with minimal human handling and full provenance. We have reproduced an agentic manipulation policy (Apple's AMP1, on the CaP-Gym benchmark) on a simulated PiPER; in simulation the agent measured and compensated joint deadbands on its own, but each task took minutes. We know of CaP-X/CaP-Gym, AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, WetRobo (a coding agent driving PiPER arms across two wet labs), Coscientist, CRESt, MATTERIX, LabSafety Bench and CADSmith.

Question.
(1) Agent-written robot code on physical laboratory hardware: which systems (2023 to 2026) have run language-model-generated code or plans on real lab robots or arms, with what measured success rates and trial counts, failure modes (unsafe or infeasible motions, wrong frames or units, hallucinated APIs, silent failures), latency and cost per task, and how often a human had to intervene?
(2) Safeguards: which verification layers have been shown to catch agent errors before or during execution (typed skill libraries, static checks, simulation or digital-twin dry runs, workspace and force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates), with measured catch rates and false-alarm rates? Is there evidence that freezing agent-written code once it works is more reliable than regenerating code for every run?
(3) Agent- or AI-designed physical hardware for laboratory robots: language-model or generative design of fixtures, holders, grippers, adapters or docking features that were then fabricated (for example 3D-printed) and tested on real hardware. Report first-pass fit or function rates, iterations to success, human edits needed, and how the designs were checked.
(4) Provenance and auditability for agent-operated laboratories: methods that link the request, the generated code or CAD, the commit, and the physical outcome (what was requested versus what physically happened), reproducibility of agent-run procedures across sites, and relevant standards (for example cybersecurity clauses in ISO 10218:2025 for networked robots).
(5) What would a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" look like: outcome metrics, baselines (human expert, scripted), sample sizes, and the failure rates the literature suggests we should expect?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, but include 2025 and 2026 preprints where they are the only evidence, flagged as preprints. For each claim give the DOI or arXiv ID and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that Chemist Eye was tested using real-world data from a self-driving laboratory equipped with three mobile robots. As a vision-language-model-powered safety monitor, it achieved 97% performance for spotting possible safety hazards and 95% performance for decision-making based on the detected issue. The system’s stated monitoring capabilities include PPE-compliance monitoring, accident detection, and fire detection, followed by robot or user-directed decision-making. The abstract describes actions such as directing mobile robots away from potential fire locations, exits, or people not wearing PPE, issuing audible warnings, and sending instant notifications through third-party messaging platforms. However, the provided pages do not report separate detection accuracies for PPE, accidents, or fires, nor do they provide false-alarm rates, confusion matrices, precision, recall, F1 scores, latency, or other detailed safety metrics. Thus, the only quantitative results available in this excerpt are the aggregate 97% hazard-spotting performance and 95% decision-making performance; any false-alarm figures or category-specific safety results would need to be obtained from later sections of the article.
contexts.question: What are the results for Chemist Eye as a vision-language model safety monitor for self-driving laboratories? What detection accuracy, false alarm rates, and safety metrics are reported?

contexts.context: LabscriptAI is a LangGraph multi-agent framework for Opentrons OT-2/OT-Flex and Hamilton Vantage robots. A Task Planning Agent conducts “human-in-the-loop dialogue” to validate protocols; Coder generates Python, while Reviewer validates it in simulators (opentrons_simulate, PyHamilton, and pyFluent). Errors trigger targeted SEARCH/REPLACE repairs, with at most nine iterations. Prompts constrain valid labware/instruments and retrieve validated code examples. The excerpt reports no physical robot trials, success/failure rates, latency, cost, intervention frequency, hardware design, runtime monitoring, provenance, or catch/false-alarm rates—only simulated code validation and configured hardware.
contexts.question:
Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab). Most remote work is done by AI coding agents: a GitHub comment starts an agent session in CI, which reaches a lab Raspberry Pi over SSH and drives the instrument (a gantry liquid handler, 3D printers, an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with Raspberry Pi cameras and AprilTags); risky actions such as starting a print wait for a human approval, and every session, command and result is recorded in the repository. The lab ran about 575 agent sessions in 30 days across seven repositories. A recent proposal of ours asks whether a language-model agent can design and validate the connecting hardware of an automated alloy-development loop (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers and fixtures, 3D-printed) and write the robot workflows around it, well enough that the loop runs with minimal human handling and full provenance. We have reproduced an agentic manipulation policy (Apple's AMP1, on the CaP-Gym benchmark) on a simulated PiPER; in simulation the agent measured and compensated joint deadbands on its own, but each task took minutes. We know of CaP-X/CaP-Gym, AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, WetRobo (a coding agent driving PiPER arms across two wet labs), Coscientist, CRESt, MATTERIX, LabSafety Bench and CADSmith.

Question.
(1) Agent-written robot code on physical laboratory hardware: which systems (2023 to 2026) have run language-model-generated code or plans on real lab robots or arms, with what measured success rates and trial counts, failure modes (unsafe or infeasible motions, wrong frames or units, hallucinated APIs, silent failures), latency and cost per task, and how often a human had to intervene?
(2) Safeguards: which verification layers have been shown to catch agent errors before or during execution (typed skill libraries, static checks, simulation or digital-twin dry runs, workspace and force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates), with measured catch rates and false-alarm rates? Is there evidence that freezing agent-written code once it works is more reliable than regenerating code for every run?
(3) Agent- or AI-designed physical hardware for laboratory robots: language-model or generative design of fixtures, holders, grippers, adapters or docking features that were then fabricated (for example 3D-printed) and tested on real hardware. Report first-pass fit or function rates, iterations to success, human edits needed, and how the designs were checked.
(4) Provenance and auditability for agent-operated laboratories: methods that link the request, the generated code or CAD, the commit, and the physical outcome (what was requested versus what physically happened), reproducibility of agent-run procedures across sites, and relevant standards (for example cybersecurity clauses in ISO 10218:2025 for networked robots).
(5) What would a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" look like: outcome metrics, baselines (human expert, scripted), sample sizes, and the failure rates the literature suggests we should expect?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, but include 2025 and 2026 preprints where they are the only evidence, flagged as preprints. For each claim give the DOI or arXiv ID and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab). Most remote work is done by AI coding agents: a GitHub comment starts an agent session in CI, which reaches a lab Raspberry Pi over SSH and drives the instrument (a gantry liquid handler, 3D printers, an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with Raspberry Pi cameras and AprilTags); risky actions such as starting a print wait for a human approval, and every session, command and result is recorded in the repository. The lab ran about 575 agent sessions in 30 days across seven repositories. A recent proposal of ours asks whether a language-model agent can design and validate the connecting hardware of an automated alloy-development loop (sample holders, docking plates, camera mounts, grippers and fixtures, 3D-printed) and write the robot workflows around it, well enough that the loop runs with minimal human handling and full provenance. We have reproduced an agentic manipulation policy (Apple's AMP1, on the CaP-Gym benchmark) on a simulated PiPER; in simulation the agent measured and compensated joint deadbands on its own, but each task took minutes. We know of CaP-X/CaP-Gym, AMP1, ACE-CaP-0, WetRobo (a coding agent driving PiPER arms across two wet labs), Coscientist, CRESt, MATTERIX, LabSafety Bench and CADSmith.

Question.
(1) Agent-written robot code on physical laboratory hardware: which systems (2023 to 2026) have run language-model-generated code or plans on real lab robots or arms, with what measured success rates and trial counts, failure modes (unsafe or infeasible motions, wrong frames or units, hallucinated APIs, silent failures), latency and cost per task, and how often a human had to intervene?
(2) Safeguards: which verification layers have been shown to catch agent errors before or during execution (typed skill libraries, static checks, simulation or digital-twin dry runs, workspace and force limits, runtime monitors, vision-language verifiers, human approval gates), with measured catch rates and false-alarm rates? Is there evidence that freezing agent-written code once it works is more reliable than regenerating code for every run?
(3) Agent- or AI-designed physical hardware for laboratory robots: language-model or generative design of fixtures, holders, grippers, adapters or docking features that were then fabricated (for example 3D-printed) and tested on real hardware. Report first-pass fit or function rates, iterations to success, human edits needed, and how the designs were checked.
(4) Provenance and auditability for agent-operated laboratories: methods that link the request, the generated code or CAD, the commit, and the physical outcome (what was requested versus what physically happened), reproducibility of agent-run procedures across sites, and relevant standards (for example cybersecurity clauses in ISO 10218:2025 for networked robots).
(5) What would a defensible evaluation of "an agent designs the fixture and writes the workflow, and the arm runs it" look like: outcome metrics, baselines (human expert, scripted), sample sizes, and the failure rates the literature suggests we should expect?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, but include 2025 and 2026 preprints where they are the only evidence, flagged as preprints. For each claim give the DOI or arXiv ID and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Agent-Written Robot Code, Safeguards, AI-Designed Hardware, Provenance, and Evaluation for Laboratory Automation: A Literature Synthesis (2023–2026)

## 1. Agent-Written Robot Code on Physical Laboratory Hardware

The period 2023–2026 has seen a rapid expansion of systems executing language-model-generated code or plans on real laboratory robots, though quantitative reporting of success rates, failure modes, latency, cost, and human intervention remains inconsistent across the literature. The following table summarizes the key systems identified.

| System | Year / status | Hardware | Task domain | Measured success rate | Trial count | Key failure modes | Latency / cost | Human intervention | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Coscientist | 2023, peer reviewed | Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler and heater–shaker; GC–MS used for outcome verification | Chemical synthesis and reaction planning | Qualitative physical success: target products verified for both Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira couplings; no defensible aggregate success rate reported | Not reported | Initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method; corrected after documentation retrieval; plates were moved manually | Not reported | No human decision-making reported, but humans manually transferred plates | DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06792-0 (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 6-6) |
| CLAIRify | 2023, peer reviewed | Franka arm with laboratory tools | Chemistry plans, pouring, solubility and recrystallization | Constrained TAMP: 97% with an 8-DoF configuration and 84% with 7 DoF; pouring relative error 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt; solubility-estimation error 7.2% | Trial denominator not reported in retrieved evidence | Invalid plan syntax or constraints, motion-planning failure, perception error, spillage and manipulation/state-assessment errors | Not reported | Intervention frequency not reported | DOI: 10.1007/s10514-023-10136-2 (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4) |
| AILA / AFMBench | 2024 preprint; 2025 peer reviewed | Atomic-force microscope | Autonomous microscopy: calibration, imaging and property measurement | Reported above 80% on multi-step workflows; exact physical trial denominator and task-level rates not available in retrieved evidence | Not reported | Prompt brittleness, wrong agent/tool selection, misunderstood context, deviation from instructions (“sleepwalking”) and actions outside requirements | Not reported | Not reported | DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-64105-7; arXiv:2501.10385 (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15) |
| MATTERIX | 2025, peer reviewed | Franka FR3 plus Opentrons OT-2 and digital twin | Chemistry-lab manipulation and liquid handling | Physical pick-and-place: 75% (9/12); physical pouring: 90% (9/10) | 22 reported physical trials across those two tests | Pose-estimation and calibration errors, wrong object frames, action failures, mismatched digital/physical assets, vessel/workspace discrepancies | Not reported | Not reported; policies were developed in simulation and transferred to hardware | DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14) |
| LabscriptAI | 2026, **bioRxiv preprint** | Opentrons OT-2/Flex, Hamilton platforms, Tecan Fluent and associated modules | Synthetic-biology liquid handling and protocol translation | 96.7% simulator-pass rate on a 90-task benchmark; physical cross-platform calibration produced CV below 5% and R² above 0.999, but no aggregate physical success rate | 90 simulated benchmark tasks; large physical campaigns included 318 GFP variants and 399 enzyme variants | Simulator/API validation errors; inadequate protein purification in one workflow; broader instrument integration remained incomplete | Per-task latency and monetary cost not reported | Human-in-the-loop dialogue validates protocols; intervention frequency not reported | DOI: 10.1101/2025.09.30.679666 (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 1-4, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 15-18, gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7) |
| WetRobo | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | AgileX PiPER arms with cameras and laboratory end effectors | Wet-lab manipulation: dish lids, caps and incubator doors | Qualitative success on real robots; cap-removal code adapted successfully in two laboratories with different grippers and camera placement; no aggregate rate | Individual adaptation trials; denominator not reported | Slipping after lid lifting, limited equipment/site generality and untested dish transport | Door opening: 2 h 40 min initial agent adaptation versus 3 min 27 s repeat execution; token/energy cost noted but not quantified | Reduced need for local teleoperation; exact intervention rate not reported | arXiv:2609.18435 (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9, oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2) |
| CaP-Agent0 / CaP-X | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Robot-manipulation stack including Franka-compatible real-robot interface; principal quoted metric is simulated LIBERO-PRO | General manipulation via agent-written policies | LIBERO-PRO averages: 11.8–25.6% under position perturbations and 14.0–18.2% under instruction perturbations; these are not physical-lab success rates | 50 trials per task in LIBERO-PRO | Mis-segmentation, occlusion, angled or failed grasps, control-API failures and collisions from absent collision-aware planning | Not reported | Not reported | arXiv:2603.22435 (fu2026capxaframework pages 56-58, fu2026capxaframework pages 7-8) |
| SPINE | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Four AgileX PiPER 6-DoF arms, ROS/CAN and RealSense cameras | Cyber-physical diagnosis and restoration of robot teleoperation | 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios versus 99% for human operators | 5 fault scenarios | Software/configuration faults, disconnected cameras or CAN links, cable/controller faults and hybrid hardware–software failures | Mean recovery 7 min 48 s versus 12 min 30 s for humans: 38% faster; cost not reported | Novice operator remained necessary for physical actions and observations | arXiv:2607.13049 (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 3-5) |
| AMP1 | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Real robot arm plus CaP-Gym simulated embodiments | General manipulation using agent-written, self-revising policies | Simulation: 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120, 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO, 100% on robosuite and 96.0% on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks; selected real tasks achieved 9/9 each | Selected physical tasks: 9 trials each; complete total not reported in retrieved evidence | Grasp failures from geometry/mass, flaky verifiers rejecting valid states and controller interruptions; AMP1 included error recovery | Selected physical tasks averaged 94–208 s; 34.8 model calls per simulated episode with full sensing; monetary cost not reported | Human-intervention rate not reported | arXiv:2611.09892 (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 4-5, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4) |
| ACE-CaP-0 | 2026, **arXiv preprint** | Real robot-arm manipulation platform | Eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs | 92.1% overall (221/240); task rates 83.3–100% | 30 trials per task; 240 total | Paper excerpt reports unsuccessful trials but no qualitative failure taxonomy | Mean physical execution 0.97–2.27 min per task; monetary cost not reported | No human or coding agent during evaluation; development allowed at most 10 human-assisted scene resets per task | arXiv:2611.16872 (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12) |


*Table: Systems that executed language-model-generated plans or code on laboratory or manipulation hardware, with simulation-only metrics clearly distinguished from physical trials. Missing latency, cost, and intervention values are marked rather than inferred.*

**Coscientist** (Boiko et al., 2023) demonstrated autonomous design and execution of Suzuki–Miyaura and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions on an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handler. The system "autonomously designed, plans and performs complex experiments" and successfully verified target products by GC–MS analysis (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 1-2). It initially hallucinated an incorrect heater–shaker API method but self-corrected after consulting documentation (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6). Safety checking blocked hazardous suggestions including sodium azide as an additive and 220°C in ethanol (ezeh2026acomprehensivereview pages 33-37). No aggregate success rate or trial count was reported; plates were moved manually (boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6).

**CLAIRify** (Yoshikawa et al., 2023) translated natural-language chemistry instructions into structured plans executed via constrained task-and-motion planning on a Franka robot. Constrained TAMP achieved 97% success with an 8-DoF robot versus 84% for 7-DoF; pouring relative errors were 8.1% for water and 8.8% for salt (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4). Failure modes included motion-planning failures, spillage, incorrect plan syntax, and perception errors (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4).

**MATTERIX** (Darvish et al., 2025) provided a GPU-accelerated digital-twin framework for chemistry laboratories. Physical pick-and-place achieved 75% success (9/12 trials) with failures from pose estimation and calibration errors; liquid pouring achieved 90% (9/10) (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14). The system validates workflows in a full simulated laboratory before physical execution (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 9-11).

**LabscriptAI** (Gao et al., 2026; *bioRxiv preprint*) achieved a 96.7% simulation-pass rate on a 90-task liquid-handling benchmark—"the highest among the evaluated LLM-based and commercial baselines" (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7). It supported four liquid-handling platforms (Opentrons OT-2, OT-Flex, Hamilton, Tecan Fluent) and demonstrated cross-platform reproducibility with CV below 5% and R² above 0.999 (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 11-15).

**WetRobo** (Oikawa et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) provided a reproducible robot kit for coding agents using PiPER arms. Cap removal was successfully adapted across two laboratories despite different grippers and camera placements; the initial adaptation took 2 h 40 min but repeat execution took only 3 min 27 s, illustrating the efficiency of code reuse (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 7-9, oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2). An alternative VLA approach failed to transfer between sites (oikawa2026wetroboareproducible pages 1-2).

**ACE-CaP-0** (2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 92.1% overall success (221/240 trials) across eight real-world manipulation tasks using frozen agent-developed programs, with no human or coding agent during evaluation. Mean physical execution time ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes per task (team2026acecap0realworldcodeaspolicies pages 9-12).

**AMP1** (Bagherieh et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 82.8–85.6% on RoboLab-120 and 95.2% on LIBERO-PRO in simulation. Selected real-world tasks achieved 9/9 success with total times of 94–208 seconds (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 4-5, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4). Failure modes included grasp failures from object geometry/mass and "flaky verifiers rejecting valid end states" (bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4).

**SPINE** (Ham et al., 2026; *arXiv preprint*) achieved 100% fault resolution across five PiPER scenarios (versus 99% for human operators using Claude Code) and reduced mean time-to-teleoperation by 38% (12 min 30 s to 7 min 48 s) (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 2-3, ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7). The strongest result was an 80% reduction in recovery time for disconnected camera and CAN links (ham2026spinebridgingthe pages 6-7).

**Common failure modes** across systems include: hallucinated or deprecated API calls (inagaki2023llmscangenerate pages 1-3, boiko2023autonomouschemicalresearch pages 5-6); perception and pose-estimation errors (yoshikawa2023largelanguagemodels pages 2-4, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14); grasp failures from object geometry (fu2026capxaframework pages 56-58, bagherieh2026onagenticmanipulation pages 3-4); wrong coordinate frames or units (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14); prompt brittleness causing substantial performance variation (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15); LLM "sleepwalking"—deviating from instructions without notification (johnson2025multiagentsystemsfor pages 12-15); and silent failures where VLM verifiers accepted failed states (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37).

**Notable gap.** Per-task latency and monetary cost are almost universally unreported, as are human-intervention rates. Only ACE-CaP-0 and AMP1 report execution times systematically.

## 2. Safeguards and Verification Layers

The following table summarizes the verification layers demonstrated in the literature.

| Safeguard layer | System / method | Mechanism | Measured effectiveness | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Static / formal checks | NeSyRo | Validates generated code with an SMT solver, checks skill preconditions with a PDDL planner, and generates probes for missing observations. | Real-robot average success was **57.5% versus 10.6%** for Code as Policies; **7 versus 53 irreversible actions**. | (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18) |
| Static / formal checks | Lang2LTL | Translates natural-language commands into temporal logic and aborts plans whose constraints are unsatisfiable. | Evaluated **52 commands**, including **12 unsatisfiable commands**, all of which were aborted. False-rejection rate was not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Static / formal checks | VASO | Model-checks induced plans against temporal-logic safety specifications using an automatically generated state-to-proposition mapping. | **96.8% specification compliance** with automatic mapping and **97.2%** with handcrafted mapping; guarantees depend on mapping correctness. | (li2026whentheworld pages 44-46) |
| Simulation / digital-twin dry run | MATTERIX | Executes hierarchical workflows in a GPU-based chemistry-laboratory digital twin, checking motion, semantic preconditions, liquids, heat transfer, and approximate reaction state before sim-to-real deployment. | Subsequent physical tests achieved **9/12 pick-and-place** and **9/10 pouring** successes; no controlled catch-rate or false-alarm comparison was reported. | (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5, darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 9-11) |
| Simulation / digital-twin dry run | ReSkill | Develops and screens programs in simulation before deploying the selected program without regeneration on hardware. | **72/80 simulated successes versus 62/80 real successes**, showing both screening value and a residual sim-to-real gap. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Simulation / API validation | LabscriptAI | Runs generated scripts in platform-specific simulators; a reviewer returns errors to a coder that applies targeted patches rather than regenerating the entire script. | Maximum of nine repair iterations; the paper reports **96.7% simulation-pass rate on 90 tasks**, but no physical-error catch rate or false-alarm rate. | (gao2025autonomousliquidhandlingrobotics pages 4-7) |
| Runtime monitor | Code-as-Monitor | Generates a VLM-based checker for spatiotemporal constraints and replans only after detecting a violation. | **88.33% success versus 76.67%** for a continuously queried baseline in simulated block stacking; explicit monitor sensitivity and false-alarm rates were not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 16-18) |
| Runtime safety filter | RoboGuard | Applies an external safety layer that rejects unsafe actions even when the underlying model is jailbroken. | Reduced unsafe execution under worst-case jailbreaks from **over 92% to below 3%**. | (li2026whentheworld pages 36-37) |
| Runtime multi-stage gates | LEASH | Separates task-level, action-level, and gripper/pouring safety gates before releasing actions. | On 92 RoboRisk tasks, reduced harm for one model from **11.23% to 0.00%** and for another from **61.23% to 12.68%**; false-alarm rate was not reported. | (li2026whentheworld pages 39-40) |
| VLM safety monitor | Chemist Eye | Uses vision-language models to detect PPE violations, accidents, and possible fires and to recommend robot or human responses. | Aggregate **97% hazard spotting** and **95% decision performance**; PPE accuracy ranged from **67.5% to 97.5%**, with format-hallucination rates of **0–1%**. Conventional false-positive rates were not reported. | (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 7-8, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 5-6, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 1-2) |
